Chapter 01Part 1 · Structure

Start with what belongs together

A convincing screen begins with relationships: what belongs together, what leads, and what the reader should notice next.

A screen has more than one kind of hierarchy

Visual hierarchy controls attention. Structural hierarchy controls behavior. A large headline may lead the eye, while a quiet parent frame determines how everything beneath it moves. Good interface design makes these hierarchies agree. The heading, explanation and action that form one idea should usually live inside one meaningful container. Otherwise the screen can look ordered while remaining fragile to edit.

Imagine a compact account panel containing a title, a balance and a date. If the title sits near one card and the date sits near another, the reader has to infer their relationship. Before changing color or font size, change the grouping. Put the title and its context together; give the value its own clear position. The composition becomes easier to understand because proximity now describes meaning.

In Paper the structural hierarchy is literal. A frame is what HTML calls a div: the layers inside it are its children, and layers that share a parent are siblings. Moving a frame moves everything inside it, and the code a developer or an agent reads has the same nesting as the layers panel. Grouping is a design decision and an implementation decision at the same time.

A useful frame groups one idea and owns one clear layout responsibility.

The principle of chapter 1

Study 01 · change it yourself
Interactive study: Hierarchy. It runs in the web edition with JavaScript.

Work at the correct level

Paper’s hover-selection update makes a normally invisible decision visible: which level of the tree receives the edit? Since June 2026, hovering highlights the top-level layer under the pointer, as in Figma. Double-clicking goes deeper, holding ⌘ reaches the innermost layer, Esc selects the parent and Enter selects the children, and ⌘ + right-click lists every layer under the pointer. A spacing change on a parent affects a relationship; a change on a child affects one object. Those are different design decisions.

Build a frame around a complete idea, then build smaller frames around its internal relationships. A page can contain a header, a content region and a footer. The content region can contain a comparison, and the comparison can contain repeated rows. These names are useful because they explain responsibility. Paper calls every new frame “Frame”, so rename it as soon as it exists by double-clicking its name on the canvas or in the layers panel. “Comparison” tells an agent and a future collaborator more than a column of identical “Frame” rows.

The layers panel lets you audit that structure at a glance. The icon beside each name gives the frame’s type: two columns for a horizontal flex frame, stacked rows for a vertical one, and dashed corners for a freeform frame whose children are placed by coordinates. Collapse all (⌥L, or right-click in the layers list) folds the tree back to its top level, and double-clicking a layer’s icon zooms the canvas to that layer. A tree that reads like an outline of the screen is a sign that the structure is sound.

Make the composition readable before decorating it

Read the canvas in three passes. First, notice the largest shapes: is there a clear primary area? Next, read only headings: do they describe a coherent sequence? Finally, inspect the small labels: can the reader tell what each number or action belongs to? These passes expose different failures. A strong overall silhouette does not compensate for a value with an ambiguous label.

Paper supports each pass. ⌘. hides every panel so the first pass sees only the canvas, and ⇧. shrinks the panels to floating pills when you still need the toolbar and the zoom level. The same thinking scales beyond one screen: pages split a file into chapters, and folders in the dashboard nest several levels deep (Marketing › Social Media › Instagram). Once the structural relationships are right, typography and color can reinforce them, and the organization still makes sense after a label grows or another row is added.

In Paper

How it works in Paper

As of September 2026, structure in Paper is HTML structure: a frame is a div and its layers are its children. Hover selects the top-level layer under the pointer; double-click, ⌘, Esc and Enter move through the tree, and ⌘ + right-click lists every layer under the pointer. ⇧F wraps layers in a freeform frame and ⇧A in a flex frame. The layers panel shows each frame’s type, pages divide a file, and the dashboard organizes files in nested folders.

Checked against the videos and documentation as of September 2026. Paper ships often; the release timeline in the reference shows what changed when.

Select at the right depth

  1. Hover over a design: Paper highlights the top-level layer under the pointer inside the artboard, not the small object you point at.
  2. Click to select that layer, or double-click to go further in (in the demo, the 334 × 300 panel, then the 206 × Fit 194 receipt inside it).
  3. Hold ⌘ while hovering or clicking to deep-select the innermost layer directly.
  4. Press Esc to select the parent of the current selection, or Enter to select its children.
  5. If you prefer hover to pick the frame closest to the pointer, click the file name at the top of the left panel and tick Use deep selection; untick it to return to the default.
Double-click⌘ClickEscEnter
Shown at 0:19

Pick a buried layer from the pointer list

  1. Place the pointer over the spot where several layers overlap.
  2. Hold ⌘ and right-click: a list opens with every layer under the pointer, indented by depth and marked with type icons (in the demo: 02 How it works, Visual, Panel, Receipt, Rectangle).
  3. Hover a row to outline that layer on the canvas.
  4. Click the row to make that layer the selection.
⌘Right-click
Shown at 1:07

Group layers into a named frame

  1. To start from an empty frame, draw one with the Frame tool and set its size, or pick a preset in the right panel (Phone, Tablet, Desktop, Presentation, Smartwatch, Paper, Social media); layers you drag into it become its children.
  2. To group existing layers, select them on the canvas or in the layers panel (Shift-click adds to the selection).
  3. Press ⇧F (Frame selection) for a freeform frame: the layers keep their positions and can be dragged anywhere inside it.
  4. Press ⇧A (Wrap in flex) for a flex frame instead. With a freeform frame selected, the same key converts it, and the button in the Layout section reads Add flex ⇧A.
  5. Double-click the frame’s name label on the canvas, or its row in the layers panel, and type a name that states its role.
⇧F⇧A
Shown at 0:50

Navigate a large layer tree

  1. Double-click a layer’s icon in the layers list: the canvas zooms to that layer and centers it.
  2. Right-click in the layers list and choose Collapse all (⌥L) to fold every group back to the top level.
  3. Hover a row to reveal its lock and eye toggles; Lock / unlock is ⇧⌘L and Show / hide is ⇧⌘H.
  4. Drag the left panel’s edge to widen it when names are long.
⌥L⇧⌘L⇧⌘H
Shown at 0:37

Split a file into pages

  1. Click + beside Pages at the top of the left panel.
  2. The new page appears (“Page 2” in a one-page file) with its name selected; type a name that describes its content.
  3. Click a page to open it; a check mark shows the page you are on.
  4. Drag pages in the list to reorder them; the pages list can also be resized by dragging its edge.
Shown at 2:26

Organize files in nested folders

  1. In the dashboard, open Files in the sidebar and click + New folder; the folder appears with its name selected (“Untitled project”), ready to type.
  2. Right-click a file card and choose Move to › a folder; the folder it is already in is grayed out.
  3. Open a folder and click + New folder again to nest another folder inside it; in Move to, folders that contain folders open a further submenu.
  4. Move a folder the same way (right-click › Move to); a toast confirms the move, for example “Moved Billboard to Marketing”.
  5. Click a level in the breadcrumb (Files / Marketing / Social Media) to go back up. Rename with right-click › Rename, or double-click the current folder’s name in the breadcrumb.

Hover selection: parent first, deeper on demand

Since this June 2026 update, Paper’s default hover matches Figma. In a mobile onboarding file, hovering a receipt illustration outlines the top-level block that contains it, not the receipt. Double-clicking went further in, to the 334 × 300 panel and then the 206 × Fit 194 receipt, and holding ⌘ deep-selects straight away. 8 Paper tips and tricks every designer should knowVideo · 3 min 46 s · 15 June 2026

Eight canvas tips

Each tip has an on-screen key overlay. ⌘. hides every panel, and ⇧. shrinks them to floating pills (file name, toolbar, avatar with Copy link and zoom). Double-clicking a layer’s icon in the layers list zooms to and centers it. ⇧F puts selected layers in a freeform frame, where they can be dragged anywhere. ⇧A on a freeform frame adds flex (the button reads Add flex ⇧A); on loose layers it wraps them in a new flex frame. In both demos the gap matched the existing spacing (12, then 22), so nothing moved. Holding ⌘ while dragging an image’s edges crops instead of resizing. Double-clicking an edge or corner, or clicking the size under the file name in Fill (1600×1200), restores the original dimensions, here 800 × 600. Right-click › Extract colors adds a “Magic Swatches” frame of 100 × 60 rectangles named by hex, such as “Color #A65C0D”. With a layer selected, I opens the eyedropper (the same tool as the icon in the color picker), and its click sets that layer’s fill.

Build it in Paper

  1. Select the layers that form one idea (Shift-click adds to the selection) and press ⇧A to wrap them in a flex frame, or ⇧F for a freeform frame. Double-click the new frame’s “Frame” label and name it for its purpose, such as “Header”.
  2. Repeat at each level: give the header, the main content and the footer their own frames as siblings inside one page-level frame, and nest smaller frames only where items share a relationship.
  3. Before changing spacing or size, confirm the level: hover shows the top-level layer, double-click goes deeper, Esc selects the parent, Enter selects the children, and ⌘ + right-click lists every layer under the pointer.
  4. Press ⌥L to collapse the layers panel and read the tree from the top: the names and icons (row, column, freeform) should follow the screen’s reading order.
  5. Duplicate a section with ⌘D, lengthen one label and check that the grouping still communicates the same hierarchy. Then file the work: in the dashboard, right-click the file and choose Move to › a named folder.

Check before you move on

  • Does every frame hold one idea, and does its name say what that idea is?
  • Before you edit spacing, can you name the selected layer and its parent?
  • With the layers panel collapsed, do the top-level frames follow the screen’s reading order?
  • If one label doubled in length, would its group still read as one unit?
  • Could a teammate find this file from its folder path and name alone?

Common mistakes

Changing gap or padding on a child because it was the layer under the pointer, when the relationship you meant lives on its parent.

Press Esc to select the parent (or ⌘ + right-click and pick it from the list), confirm its name in the layers panel, then edit.

Leaving every container named “Frame”, so the layers panel, prompts and handoff notes cannot tell sections apart.

Rename each frame when you create it: double-click its name on the canvas or in the layers panel and describe its role.

Using ⇧F for a group whose items should reflow, so the children keep fixed coordinates when content changes.

Use ⇧A for groups that should stay arranged; to fix an existing freeform frame, select it and press ⇧A (Add flex).

Leaving files loose in Files, where old versions sit next to current work.

Create folders with + New folder, nest them by product or theme, and move files with right-click › Move to.

Chapter 02Part 1 · Structure

Make space follow the content

Flex layout turns a collection of objects into a relationship that can survive longer labels, extra rows and changing dimensions.

From placed objects to a rule

A manually placed icon and label can look perfect at one moment. Change the label, and their relationship has to be repaired. A layout rule solves the more general problem: the icon occupies its lane, the text takes the space it needs, and the distance between them stays intentional. You are designing the response to change as well as the current picture.

Paper’s Flex lesson builds from a menu item to a sidebar. Pressing ⇧A (Wrap in flex) gives a new parent frame responsibility for arranging the selected layers. Direction defines the reading axis; gap separates siblings; padding creates an inner boundary. These controls describe three different relationships. Increasing padding to fix a gap may improve one screenshot while making the surrounding component feel wrong.

Paper calls the feature flex rather than auto layout because its canvas is built on HTML and CSS, and agents and developers already use that vocabulary. A flex frame is a div laid out with CSS flexbox, so the gap, padding and alignment you set in the panel are the same properties a developer or an agent reads in the code.

Gap separates siblings, padding protects content, and sizing declares a dependency.

The principle of chapter 2

Study 02 · change it yourself
Interactive study: Flex. It runs in the web edition with JavaScript.

Size is a dependency

Fixed, Fit and Fill answer a simple question: what determines this dimension? A Fixed value follows the designer’s decision. Fit follows the content. Fill follows the space left in the parent. Their usefulness comes from combining them deliberately. In a menu row, the icon can keep a stable width while the label receives the remaining room; the row’s height can follow its content. Paper’s instructions for agents make the same point about repeated rows: give icons and trailing actions fixed-width slots that do not shrink, because gap alone will not line up columns from row to row.

A parent that follows its child and a child that follows its parent can create an unclear sizing relationship. When a layout behaves unexpectedly, read the size badge under the selection, which names each axis’s mode (for example “Fill 267 × Fit 317”), before nudging coordinates. Decide where the available space originates. A page establishes a content width; a row fills that width; its icon keeps its own size; its text uses the space left over. The explanation should be easy to say aloud.

Space between distributes available space among siblings. It does not know which siblings form a conceptual group. If an icon, label and trailing value must become two visual groups, nest the icon and label together first with ⇧A. The outer row can then separate the leading group from the value. This is the central move in the tutorial: correct grouping makes an alignment control produce the intended result.

Exceptions should be visible

Some objects do not belong in normal flow. A close button over the corner of a panel should not push the panel’s content aside. Paper’s example ticks Absolute position on such a button: it leaves the flow and sits on top of the content, but it keeps its default Left and Top constraints, so it drifts when the banner is resized until you pin it to the right edge. Treat that as an explicit exception, not a general way to position every item on the screen.

Paper keeps these choices inspectable. The layers panel marks rows, columns and freeform frames with different icons, and since September 2026 a flex layout written by an agent opens in the same Flex panel, ready to edit. A small, meaningful nested frame can remove several arbitrary offsets. When a row can explain where its dimensions come from, the same structure becomes easier to duplicate, adapt to a narrower surface and translate into implementation.

In Paper

How it works in Paper

Paper’s Flex is CSS flexbox: a flex frame is a div with display: flex. As of September 2026, the Flex section sets direction, wrap, gap (one gap between items and another between lines once wrapped), padding per axis or per side, nine-point alignment, Space between and baseline alignment. Each axis is Fixed, Fit (follows its content, like fit-content) or Fill (takes the parent’s remaining space). ⇧A wraps or converts; Absolute position takes a child out of the flow.

Checked against the videos and documentation as of September 2026. Paper ships often; the release timeline in the reference shows what changed when.

Wrap layers in a flex frame

  1. Select the layers that should move together; Shift-click adds to the selection.
  2. Press ⇧A, or click Wrap in flex ⇧A in the right panel’s Layout section.
  3. The new parent is named “Frame”, laid out as a row and sized Fit on both axes, with a starting gap (8 in the demo); the badge under it reads, for example, “Fit 116 × Fit 32”.
  4. Rename it by double-clicking its name on the canvas or in the layers panel (“Menu Button” in the demo).
  5. To convert an existing freeform frame instead, select it and press ⇧A; the button then reads Add flex. To remove flex, click − in the Flex header or press ⌥⇧A.
⇧A⌥⇧A⇧Click
Shown at 1:37

Set gap and padding

  1. Select the parent frame: gap and padding belong to it, not to the children.
  2. Set the gap (tooltip “Gap between elements”): type a value; or press ↑ or ↓ to change it by 1, and with ⇧ by the nudge amount (8 in the demo, set in Nudge settings… in the file-name menu).
  3. Or drag the gap field’s icon left or right, or drag the pink band between two children directly on the canvas; a badge shows the value.
  4. Set the horizontal and vertical padding (8 and 8 in the demo).
  5. Click the square icon at the end of the padding row to set each side separately; click it again to return to one value per axis.
↑⇧↑
Shown at 2:08

Change direction, order and alignment

  1. Click ↓ to stack the children in a column, or → for a row; the children keep their order either way.
  2. To reorder, drag a child (a blue line marks where it will land) or select it and press the arrow keys.
  3. Click one of the nine points to align the children inside the frame; the demo settles on left, vertically centered.
  4. For Space between, open the sliders icon in the Flex section and choose Space between, or double-click the nine-point grid.
→Double-click
Shown at 4:12

Keep related items together under Space between

  1. Spot the symptom: with three children, Space between pushes the middle one to the center.
  2. Shift-click the items that belong together (avatar and name), press ⇧A and set their gap (8).
  3. Name the new frame for its role (“User info”). The parent now has two children, so the group sits at one end and the chevron at the other.
  4. To stack text inside the group, select the name and the email, press ⇧A, click ↓ and set the gap to 0.
  5. In a vertical sidebar, the same move keeps a top group at the top and a user button at the bottom: set the sidebar to Space between and wrap the brand and the navigation with ⇧A (gap 24).
⇧Click⇧A
Shown at 6:38

Size with Fixed, Fit and Fill

  1. Fixed: drag an edge, type a value in W or H, or press the arrow keys in the field.
  2. Fit: choose Fit in the W or H dropdown, or double-click the frame’s top or bottom edge to set the height to Fit.
  3. Fill: choose Fill, or hold ⌥ and double-click the left or right edge; the layer then takes the parent’s unused width (badge “Fill 267 × Fit 317” in the demo).
  4. To let a child drive its parent, set the parent’s W to Fit: when the fixed-width child changes (220 to 300 in the demo), the parent follows, and siblings set to Fill follow the parent.
Double-click⌥Double-click
Shown at 9:52

Wrap children onto new lines (September 2026 panel)

  1. Select the frame that directly contains the items, such as a row of cards or tags.
  2. Click the wrap toggle, the curved-arrow icon beside the direction buttons; items that no longer fit move to a new line.
  3. Set the gap between items in the first gap field and the gap between lines in the second field that appears (16 and 20 in the demo).
  4. To see which items overflow before wrapping, you can turn off Clip content (⌥C) on the outer frame.
⌥C
Shown at 3:33

From a menu button to a responsive sidebar

Selecting an avatar and a name and pressing ⇧A wraps them in a flex frame (Fit × Fit, gap 8), renamed “Menu Button”. Gap is typed, stepped with arrow keys (⇧ for bigger steps), or dragged from its field icon or the pink band on the canvas. A dropped chevron lands at the blue line; arrow keys reorder it. A “muted” token fill, padding 8 × 8 and radius 8 follow, and ↓ stacks the children in order. A double-click on the bottom edge sets the height to Fit; the width stays fixed at 220. Space between strands the name mid-row, so avatar and name get their own ⇧A frame, “User info”, and name and email a ↓ frame with gap 0. A sidebar repeats the move, keeping the button at the bottom. Fill (⌥ + double-click an edge) makes the navigation follow the sidebar; on a Fit sidebar, widening the button to 300 resizes both. 1:37Wrap in flex ⇧A2:24Drag the gap on the canvas5:46Fit height, fixed width6:38Nested frame for Space between9:52Fill and Fit sizing11:54Absolute position

Build it in Paper

  1. Select an avatar image and a name and press ⇧A (or click Wrap in flex ⇧A in the Layout section). Double-click the new frame’s name and call it “Menu Button”; leave the direction on → (row).
  2. With the parent selected, set the gap to 8, horizontal and vertical padding to 8 and the radius to 8, then add a fill, ideally from a color token.
  3. Drag a chevron icon into the frame (a blue line shows where it will land). Fix the width at 220, then double-click the bottom edge to set the height to Fit.
  4. Choose Space between from the sliders icon (or double-click the alignment grid). When the name drifts to the middle, Shift-click the avatar and the name, press ⇧A, set that frame’s gap to 8 and name it “User info”.
  5. Place the button at the bottom of a vertical sidebar set to Space between, wrap the sidebar’s top items with ⇧A, give the navigation group Fill width (⌥ + double-click its side edge) and resize the sidebar to test.

Check before you move on

  • For every frame, can you say where its width and height come from: Fixed, Fit or Fill?
  • If the longest label doubled, would anything overlap, clip or jump to a new position?
  • Is every space between siblings a gap and every inner margin padding, with no spacer layers or nudged offsets?
  • Does each Space between parent contain only the children that should be pushed apart?
  • Is anything on Absolute position that should be in the flow, and is every overlay pinned to the edges it belongs to?

Common mistakes

Applying Space between to a row of three children and getting the middle one stranded in the center.

Group the items that belong together with ⇧A first, so the parent has exactly the children that should be pushed apart.

Widening padding, or adding spacer rectangles, to fix the distance between two siblings.

Set the parent’s gap for space between siblings, and keep padding for the frame’s inner boundary.

Dropping a new item into a top-aligned flex frame and expecting it to stay where you released it.

Flex places children by order: watch the blue insertion line, reorder with the arrow keys, or group and use Space between to pin an item to one end.

Placing a close button with Absolute position and assuming it will stay in the corner.

It keeps Left and Top constraints by default; pin it to the top and right edges, then resize the parent to test.

Chapter 03Part 1 · Structure

Use alignment to make comparison effortless

A grid is a set of shared positions. Its value is the reading work it removes, especially when people compare numbers.

An edge can be more useful than a box

When repeated values begin or end at different positions, the eye must search before it can compare. A shared edge removes that search. This is why a calm table often communicates more than a wall of individually polished cards. The reader can travel down a value lane or across a category without reinterpreting the layout at every stop.

Alignment is not the same as centering. A centered value may look balanced inside its own card while being difficult to compare with values elsewhere. Choose the edge that serves the task. Text labels usually need a predictable starting point. Numbers benefit from a consistent ending point and, where the typeface supports them, tabular numerals. Units and qualifiers need positions that remain attached to the values they describe.

Align the content that people compare, not merely the boxes that contain it.

The principle of chapter 3

Study 03 · change it yourself
Interactive study: Alignment. It runs in the web edition with JavaScript.

Build a visual grid with available tools

As of early October 2026, Paper's public roadmap lists native CSS Grid authoring as planned, not shipped. You can still design a precise visual grid with nested Flex frames: a vertical Flex stack of rows, each row a horizontal Flex frame whose children are the lanes. Grid layouts that arrive from code, such as a section captured with Snapshot, still render on the canvas, and the September 2026 release added alignment and gap support for grid elements. The shipped page may use browser Grid, Flex or a semantic table; the design principle is the same shared geometry.

Decide the lanes once, then repeat them. If each row chooses its own label width, the apparent grid drifts as soon as one label grows. Give every value lane the same Fixed width and let the label take the remaining width with Fill. Paper's instructions for agents make the same point in CSS terms: gap alone won't align columns across rows, so repeated rows need fixed-width slots that do not shrink. Use padding to keep values off the edges of their lane, and reserve larger gaps for transitions between genuinely different groups.

Once alignment supplies the order, emphasis can stay selective: a pale band behind one group, or a single accent color for the value that matters. Check the order before you add emphasis. In Paper, hold ⌥ with a layer selected to read its distances to the parent's edges, and read the size badge under the selection, which names each axis's mode, as in "Fill 387.33 × Fit 201.92". The menu under the file name toggles Layout guides (⇧G), Show pixel grid (⌘') and Snap to pixel (⇧⌘').

Test the row that makes the layout uncomfortable

A grid should be judged with a long label, an absent value and a value with an unfamiliar number of digits. These cases reveal whether the apparent order comes from the structure or from conveniently short content. An absent observation should keep its place and show an explicit missing state. Removing the cell destroys the comparison precisely where explanation is most needed.

Paper's Snapshot iteration tutorial shows why that review belongs on the canvas. An agent added a third column to a captured section: it changed the grid from repeat(2, 1fr) to three columns, duplicated a column and reported a passing checkpoint review, including that all three columns sat properly on the grid. The new column still had an empty image area, and the media frames kept a fixed height of 324 that now left too much empty space. The presenter fixed each frame by double-clicking its bottom edge to set Fit. Duplication preserves structure, but it also creates new relationships that only a look at the actual rows can confirm.

In Paper

How it works in Paper

As of September 2026, Paper builds grids from nested Flex frames: a vertical stack of rows, each a horizontal Flex frame whose lanes are Fixed, Fit or Fill. Gap, padding and the nine-point alignment grid map to CSS gap, padding, justify-content and align-items. The September flex-panel rework put Space between beside the gap field, split the wrap gap into separate horizontal and vertical values, and added alignment and gap for grid elements. Native CSS Grid authoring remains planned on the roadmap.

Checked against the videos and documentation as of September 2026. Paper ships often; the release timeline in the reference shows what changed when.

Build a row with shared lanes

  1. Select the label and value text layers and press ⇧A, or click "Wrap in flex ⇧A" in the right panel's Layout section.
  2. In the new frame's Flex section, check the direction: → lays children out in a row, ↓ in a column.
  3. Select one value and press ⇧A again to give it a lane frame of its own; repeat for each value.
  4. Type the same number into W for every value lane so each one is Fixed.
  5. Set the label's W to Fill in the W dropdown (Fixed, Fit, Fill, Relative), or hold ⌥ and double-click its left or right edge.
  6. Read the size badge under the selection to confirm each mode, for example "Fill 267 × Fit 317".
⇧A⌥Double-click
Shown at 1:36

Stack rows into a column and space them

  1. Select the finished row and press ⇧A, then click ↓ in the new frame's Flex section so rows stack.
  2. Select the row and press ⌘D for each extra row you need.
  3. With the column selected, set the gap: type a value, use ↑ and ↓ (hold ⇧ for the nudge step), drag the field's icon, or drag the pink gap band on the canvas.
  4. Set horizontal and vertical padding; the square icon at the end of the padding row switches to four separate sides.
  5. When you drag a layer into a Flex frame, a blue outline marks the receiving frame and a blue line marks where the layer will land.
⇧A⌘D
Shown at 2:04

Align content inside a lane

  1. Select the lane frame, not the text inside it.
  2. Click a point on the Flex section's nine-point grid. In a row lane, the right-hand middle point ends the number on the lane's right edge and centers it vertically.
  3. To push the last child to the far edge, turn on Space between. In the July 2026 panel it sat in the sliders menu, and double-clicking the grid did the same; since September it is in the menu of the button beside the gap field.
  4. If Space between scatters three children, select the two that belong together and press ⇧A so the parent has only two children.
Double-click⇧A
Shown at 5:59

Line up freeform and absolute layers with the align buttons

  1. Select a child of a freeform frame, or a child with Absolute position ticked.
  2. Use the align buttons in the Layout section header: left, horizontal centers, right, top, vertical centers and bottom, followed by a … button.
  3. Align horizontal centers shows the shortcut ⌥⇧S in its tooltip.
  4. The two centering buttons also set that axis's constraint to Center, so the layer stays centered when its parent is resized.
  5. Hold ⌥ to read the distances to the parent's edges and confirm the result.
⌥⇧S⌥
Shown at 1:46

Have an agent extend a grid, then review the rows yourself

  1. Place the new content in a small frame beside the design, so the agent can read it from the canvas instead of from the prompt.
  2. Start the prompt with the location, as the tutorial does with "In Paper, add a third column to the frame", then name the frame or text that holds the new content.
  3. Approve the write tools when the agent asks; the Claude app offers Allow once (↵) and Always allow for project (local) (⌘↵).
  4. Read the agent's review, then inspect the canvas yourself for empty media areas, heights that no longer fit and text that wraps differently.
  5. Select each oversized frame and double-click its bottom edge to set its height to Fit.
Double-click
Shown at 0:37

Edit wrapped and grid layouts in the September 2026 flex panel

  1. Select a Flex frame. The reworked Flex section shows the nine-point grid on the left, the ↓ and → direction buttons on the right with a wrap toggle beside them, and the gap field below.
  2. Click the wrap toggle to let children flow onto new lines; a second gap field appears, so horizontal and vertical gaps are set separately (16 and 20 in the demo).
  3. Open the button beside the gap field for Space between, with an axis option (Vertically on a column frame), and Align to baseline, with First baseline and Last baseline.
  4. Layouts that an agent builds with Flex now open in this panel too, and grid elements support alignment and gap.

0:37Prompt starts with "In Paper"1:34Allow Duplicate Nodes1:52repeat(2, 1fr) becomes three columns2:12Checkpoint review passes2:34Missing image noticed2:53Double-click edge sets Fit

Build it in Paper

  1. Create one row first: a label text and two value texts. Select them and press ⇧A (Wrap in flex), then check that the new frame's Flex section shows → for a row.
  2. Select each value and press ⇧A again so it sits in a lane frame of its own. Type the same number into W for both value lanes so they are Fixed, then set the label's W to Fill, or hold ⌥ and double-click its left or right edge.
  3. Select each value lane and click the right-hand middle point of the nine-point grid so the number ends on the lane's right edge. Set the row's gap and its padding as separate values.
  4. Select the row, press ⇧A and click ↓ to start a column of rows, then select the row and press ⌘D for each extra row. Replace one label with a long phrase and one value with an explicit missing state.
  5. Drag the outer frame's edge to resize it, hold ⌥ to read distances, and confirm that every value lane keeps the same right edge in every row.

Check before you move on

  • Does every value end on the same edge in every row, including the row with the longest label?
  • Do all value lanes share one Fixed width, so that no row sets its own geometry?
  • Does a missing value keep its cell and say explicitly that it is missing?
  • Is the padding inside a lane smaller than the gap between groups?
  • After an agent changed the grid, did you check images, heights and wrapping on the canvas itself?

Common mistakes

Centering each number inside its own card, so every card looks balanced but the values sit at different positions.

Put the values in lanes of one Fixed width and align them to the lane's right edge with the nine-point grid.

Relying on gap alone to line up columns across rows.

Give each repeated lane a Fixed width; gap only spaces neighbors, it does not create columns.

Turning on Space between in a row of three children and getting a middle item that floats to the center.

Select the items that belong together and press ⇧A so the parent has two children, then apply Space between.

Treating an agent's passing self-review as proof that the grid is finished.

Inspect the rows on the canvas. In the tutorial the review passed while a column lacked its image and the media frames kept an outdated fixed height.

Chapter 04Part 1 · Structure

Design what happens when the frame changes

Responsive design is the preservation of meaning as space changes, not a smaller copy of the desktop composition.

Decide which relationship must survive

A desktop layout has room to separate many things at once. On a phone, that arrangement may no longer fit, but the reader still needs the same essential relationships: a label beside its meaning, an action near the decision it completes, and a route back to the previous state. A responsive design preserves those relationships even when the geometry changes.

Begin with the content's limits. A row that contains a rank, portrait, name and score has several different requirements. The portrait should remain recognizable; the score should remain comparable; the name may wrap. Squeezing every dimension equally ignores these differences. A better small-screen composition gives each element a clear rule, then allows the surrounding structure to adapt.

Responsive rules protect the important relationships while allowing the arrangement to change.

The principle of chapter 4

Study 04 · change it yourself
Interactive study: Constraints. It runs in the web edition with JavaScript.

Flow and constraints solve different problems

Flex governs relationships among participating siblings. Constraints govern how a layer outside that flow responds when its parent is resized: a child of a frame without Flex, or a child with Absolute position ticked inside a Flex frame. Paper's constraints tutorial makes the distinction tangible with a corner close button and a centered modal. The close button belongs to an edge relationship; the modal belongs to a center relationship. Neither behavior is described by where it happens to sit in one screenshot.

The tutorial also distinguishes Center, Left + Right and Stretch. Center keeps the child's width and lets the space on each side change. Left + Right keeps the distance to both edges, so the child's width changes instead. Stretch scales the width and the side distances together, and Paper then shows the width as a percentage. These are different promises. For a reading panel, comfortable content dimensions usually matter more than proportional scaling.

A design can require a structural change beyond simple resizing. Two comparison columns may become labeled groups; a toolbar may wrap; a long description may move beneath its title. Paper frames at selected widths can specify those outcomes, and since August 2026 a Flex frame can also wrap its children onto new lines. The frames are design evidence for the implementation, not proof that the running application already switches correctly between them.

Use demanding content at more than one width

Compare the same content under different space conditions. Keep the wording constant while changing width, so the effect of the layout rule remains visible. In Paper, duplicate the frame and drag the copy's edge or type a new W. When an agent creates artboards through the Paper MCP, its default sizes are Desktop 1440 × 900, Tablet 768 × 1024 and Mobile 390 × 844. Then replace one short label with a longer one. If both variables change at once, it becomes difficult to tell whether an improvement came from the structure or from friendlier content.

A narrow layout also changes interaction. A persistent navigation bar occupies valuable height but keeps the user oriented; a floating control may cover the last item unless the content accounts for it. These are part of the responsive composition. The most useful review therefore follows a complete task from its entry point to its result, including the last row and the state after an action.

In Paper

How it works in Paper

As of September 2026, Paper handles a resized parent in two ways. Flex children follow the parent's direction, gap and alignment and their own Fixed, Fit or Fill sizes; since August 2026 they can also wrap. Layers outside Flex flow, meaning children of freeform frames and children with Absolute position ticked, follow constraints: Left, Right, Left + Right, Center or Stretch horizontally, a matching vertical choice, and a pin diagram. Stretch expresses the width as a percentage of the parent.

Checked against the videos and documentation as of September 2026. Paper ships often; the release timeline in the reference shows what changed when.

Pin an overlay to a corner

  1. Select the overlay inside its Flex frame (a 16 × 16 close button in the demo) and tick Absolute position in the right panel; it leaves the flow and floats over the content.
  2. Hold ⌥ to read its distances and place it; the Flex tutorial used 16 from the top and 16 from the right.
  3. Note the starting constraints: Paper sets Left and Top, so the button drifts away from the corner when the parent widens.
  4. Click the right handle of the constraints diagram (its tooltips read like "Pin top"), or open the horizontal dropdown and choose Right. Leave the vertical dropdown on Top.
  5. Resize the parent: the button now keeps the same distance from the top and from the right.
⌥
Shown at 1:05

Keep an overlay centered

  1. Select the overlay inside a frame without Flex; in the demo, a Transfer modal inside a freeform frame named Modal scrim.
  2. Do not rely on dragging: a red guide appears when the modal reaches the middle, but its constraints stay Left and Top.
  3. Click Align horizontal centers (⌥⇧S) in the Layout section header; the horizontal constraint changes to Center.
  4. Click Align vertical centers; the vertical constraint changes to Center as well.
  5. Resize the parent: the overlay keeps its size and stays centered.
⌥⇧S
Shown at 1:46

Choose how the width responds

  1. Select the overlay and open the horizontal constraint dropdown: Left, Right, Left + Right, Center, Stretch.
  2. Center keeps the width and lets the space on each side change.
  3. Left + Right keeps both side distances and lets the width change; hold ⌥ to read them (500 on each side in the demo).
  4. Stretch changes the width and the side distances in proportion, and the W field then shows a percentage (36% in the demo).
  5. Set the vertical dropdown the same way; in the demo, the full-size scrim used Left + Right with Top + Bottom.
⌥
Shown at 2:30

Make Flex children follow their parent

  1. Select a child that should grow and set its W to Fill, or hold ⌥ and double-click its left or right edge.
  2. Keep items that must hold their size, such as an avatar or a score column, on Fixed.
  3. Double-click a frame's top or bottom edge to set its height to Fit, so it follows its content.
  4. To let one child set a column's width, set the parent's W to Fit; siblings on Fill then follow the parent.
  5. Resize the outer frame and watch which children grow, shrink or keep their size.
⌥Double-clickDouble-click
Shown at 9:40

Let a row wrap

  1. If items are cut off, untick Clip content (⌥C) on the outer frame to see the overflow.
  2. Select the direct parent of the items; in the August 2026 demo, a row of genre pills on a 390-wide phone screen.
  3. Turn on wrap: in the August panel, choose Wrap in the sliders menu; in the September panel, click the wrap toggle beside the direction arrows.
  4. Reorder items to change where lines break; an item that does not fit wraps at its own position.
  5. In the September panel, set the horizontal and vertical gaps separately while wrap is on.
⌥C
Shown at 4:14

Test a frame at more than one width

  1. Duplicate the frame with ⌘D so the original stays as a reference.
  2. Resize the copy by dragging an edge or typing a new W; when you draw a new frame, the right panel lists presets such as Phone, Tablet and Desktop.
  3. Check Fill children, wrapped rows and pinned overlays, and hold ⌥ to confirm distances to the edges.
  4. Replace one short label with a long one and look at the last row at the narrowest width.

Limits and what is coming

  • Constraints apply only outside Flex flow. A Flex child ignores them and responds through its Fixed, Fit or Fill size and its parent's Flex settings.
  • Ticking Absolute position starts a layer at Left and Top, and dragging a layer to the visual center leaves its constraints unchanged; in the July 2026 demo, only the align buttons set Center automatically.
  • Paper can store breakpoint values as tokens, but as of September 2026 the tutorials show no way to switch one frame between layouts at a breakpoint; you design each width as its own frame, and the implementation decides how one becomes the other.
  • There was no scale tool as of 28 September 2026 (announced as coming soon), so resizing a frame changes its layout but does not scale its contents. A lock for the aspect ratio of an existing frame was also described as coming soon in a team reply at the start of October 2026.

What the tutorials show

Each official video, written down step by step. The timestamps open the video at that moment, if you want to see it.

Constraints in PaperVideo · 3 min 31 s · 20 July 2026

3:31

Pin a close button, center a modal, compare Center, Left + Right and Stretch

Part two of Paper's layout series defines constraints as the rules for a layer that is not a Flex item: a child of a frame without Flex, or a child with Absolute position inside a Flex frame. When the banner card from the Flex tutorial widens, its absolute close button stays behind, because Paper pinned it Left and Top. Under W and H sit a horizontal dropdown, a vertical dropdown and a constraints diagram; clicking the diagram's right handle sets Right, and the button holds the top-right corner. Next, a Transfer modal inside a freeform Modal scrim stays Left and Top even after being dragged to the middle. Align horizontal centers, then Align vertical centers, switch both constraints to Center. With Left + Right, holding ⌥ shows 500 on each side, and those margins hold while the modal widens. With Stretch, the margins and the width change together and W reads 36%.

0:35Close button drifts on resize1:00Dropdowns and pin diagram1:06Horizontal options; Right chosen1:48Align buttons set Center/Center2:36Left + Right keeps 500 each side3:00Stretch: W becomes 36%

Build it in Paper

  1. Build the screen from Flex frames and give each child a size mode by its job: Fill for text that should grow, Fixed for a portrait or a score column, Fit for a frame that should hug its content.
  2. For a close button or badge that floats over content, tick Absolute position, then click the right handle of the constraints diagram (or choose Right in the horizontal dropdown) and keep Top.
  3. For a modal inside a freeform frame, click Align horizontal centers (⌥⇧S) and Align vertical centers in the Layout section header so both constraints read Center; on a copy, try Left + Right and Stretch to compare.
  4. Duplicate the frame with ⌘D, drag the copy's edge to a narrow width, and hold ⌥ with an overlay selected to confirm its distances to the edges.
  5. Swap in a long name, check the last row and any floating control at the narrow width, and turn on wrap for rows of variable-length items.

Check before you move on

  • For each floating layer, which edges should it keep its distance to, and do its constraints say so?
  • Were overlays centered with the align buttons, so that their constraints read Center?
  • Which children should grow (Fill), keep their size (Fixed) or hug their content (Fit)?
  • At the narrowest width, are the last row, the navigation and every overlay still usable?
  • Between comparisons, did you change only the width and keep the content identical?

Common mistakes

Placing a close button in the corner by hand after ticking Absolute position and assuming it will stay there.

Pin Right and Top in the constraints diagram or dropdowns, then resize the parent to check.

Dragging a modal to the middle of its frame and calling it centered.

Use Align horizontal centers and Align vertical centers, which also set both constraints to Center.

Choosing Stretch for a reading panel, so its line length grows with the screen.

Use Center to keep the width, or Left + Right when fixed margins matter more than a fixed width.

Expecting constraints to control a child that is still in Flex flow.

Change the child's Fixed, Fit or Fill mode or the parent's Flex settings, or tick Absolute position if the child should float.

Part 2

Visual language

Tokens give type, color and spacing their roles; charts make numbers easy to judge; vectors have to work at the size people actually see them.

3 chapters, 3 live studies
10 source videos, 36 minutes, written down

Chapter 05Part 2 · Visual language

Give the interface a consistent visual language

Tokens make decisions reusable. Typography makes those decisions visible in the rhythm, emphasis and density of the page.

Name the role before choosing the value

A palette is a collection of colors. A design language explains what those colors mean. A red swatch may be an identity accent, a destructive action or an error signal. If one token carries all three roles, changing the brand can unintentionally change the language of feedback. Semantic names make that conflict visible before it spreads across a product.

Start with a small set of roles: page background, content surface, primary text, secondary text, boundary, action and selected state. These are proposed concepts, not a mandatory token vocabulary. Their value comes from consistency. A boundary token should describe a separator’s purpose rather than the particular gray selected on the first day of the project.

Paper supports this split directly. Each token is a CSS custom property such as --color-action, and its value can be another token written as var(--color-blue-500), so a semantic role can alias a palette color and a brand change happens in one place. Through the MCP, a token can also carry a description of up to 1,024 characters, a good home for its role. Paper’s team showed why roles matter: after the accent and gold tokens became teal, a related token still carried the name gold, and the new teal sat close to the success green.

Tokens preserve decisions; typography gives those decisions a readable hierarchy.

The principle of chapter 5

Study 05 · change it yourself
Interactive study: Tokens and type. It runs in the web edition with JavaScript.

Typography creates hierarchy through relationships

A useful type system does more than list font sizes. It explains how a page title differs from a section heading, how a label differs from a paragraph, and how a number behaves next to its unit. Weight, line height, width and spacing all participate. Enlarging a title can establish emphasis, but reducing competing emphasis elsewhere can achieve the same clarity with less visual noise.

Compact interfaces need especially deliberate typography. Smaller text does not automatically create useful density; it can simply make weak hierarchy harder to read. Keep the primary values easy to find, give labels sufficient contrast and use restrained differences between secondary levels. Paper’s agent guide (October 2026) asks for higher contrast below 16 px and accepts text of 12 px or smaller only in dense productivity interfaces or as an all-caps effect. Variable fonts help with restraint: a weight of 560 can sit between Medium and Semibold instead of forcing a jump.

Paper’s CSS-variable tutorial imports an existing vocabulary, has an agent draw a style guide board and then checks the bindings on real layers. A specimen is valuable because it shows roles together. An action color that looks fine alone may be too similar to success; a muted label may disappear on a tinted surface. Design the relationships in a visible specimen before applying them throughout a flow.

A binding should have an intended scope

Changing a token inside a Paper file updates every layer bound to it, whether you edit it in the Theme tab or an agent calls set_tokens. Copying a theme to another file creates an independent set, so cross-file consistency requires a deliberate synchronization process. This distinction affects how you organize experiments. A separate file can protect an alternative, while a shared token inside one file can intentionally keep several screens moving together.

Detaching is the usual way a binding loses its scope. A detached fill becomes a literal value that later token edits skip, which is exactly what an agent warned about after Paper’s team recolored two elements by hand. Before you change a token, select the frame and read Selection colors in the right panel: bound colors appear as token names, stray ones as hex values, each with a usage count. Typography deserves the same discipline. A font available in Paper must also be available to the implemented product; otherwise line breaks and component heights may change even when the exported sizes are identical.

In Paper

How it works in Paper

As of September 2026, Paper tokens are named CSS custom properties stored per file, in eleven types that follow Tailwind v4: color, opacity, font family, font weight, font size, line height, letter spacing, spacing, radius, container and breakpoint. You create and edit them in the Theme tab, from a fill’s token menu, or through the MCP (create_tokens, set_tokens, get_tokens). Layers reference them as var(--name), so edits propagate within the file. Copy theme moves a snapshot to another file; modes, theme classes and libraries had not shipped.

Checked against the videos and documentation as of September 2026. Paper ships often; the release timeline in the reference shows what changed when.

Create tokens with an agent, from code or from a frame

  1. Open the target file in Paper Desktop. In June 2026 the agent simply worked on the open file; since tabs arrived in August, name the file in the prompt, as in “In Paper, in the finance app file, …”.
  2. From the repository, prompt: “Create tokens in the open Paper file based on the CSS variables in this codebase.” To start from a design instead, point at a frame: “create color tokens based on the color swatch frame” (August 2026 demo).
  3. Expect Get Guide, Get Basic Info and Get Tokens first, then Create Tokens calls batched by category. Approve them if your agent asks; Cursor showed Allowlist MCP Tool and Run.
  4. Each create_tokens entry needs type, name and value, plus an optional description: {"type": "color", "name": "--color-action", "value": "var(--color-blue-500)"}. Create palette tokens before the aliases that point at them.
  5. Read the summary. The June demo reported 96 tokens (65 colors, 16 typography, 10 radius, 5 spacing and layout) with their source files; light-dark() values kept only the light value, and Paper rewrote --text-xs--line-height as --text-xs-line-height.
  6. Spot-check on the canvas: draw a rectangle, click the four-circle Color tokens button beside the Fill color and pick a token.
Shown at 0:18

Create and edit tokens in the Theme tab

  1. In the left panel, switch from Design to Theme. The tab shows the token count, a Search tokens field and +.
  2. Click + and pick a type: Color, Opacity, Radius, Spacing, Container, Breakpoint, Font family, Font weight, Font size, Line height or Letter spacing. Opacity joined the list in September 2026.
  3. The new Untitled token opens in an editor with a preview, Name and Value. Type a name; for a font family, Value opens a picker with Fonts, Favorites and Tokens tabs, and starred fonts appear under Favorites.
  4. To edit a token, click it. Value can be another token, which makes an alias, or a color from the picker; compare Previous and New, then close the editor to save. Every bound layer in the file updates.
  5. To capture a color already on the canvas (September 2026), select a layer with a raw fill, click the token button beside the fill value and press + at the top of the token menu, then name the new Untitled token in the Theme tab.
⌘F
Shown at 2:26

Apply, swap and detach tokens on a layer

  1. Select the layer and click the four-circle button beside the Fill color (tooltip Color tokens). Pick a token; the field becomes a chip such as accent, with a broken-link detach icon beside it.
  2. Reopen the menu to swap tokens, or click the detach icon to get a plain hex value you can edit in the color picker.
  3. For text, open the size or line-height dropdown: tokens are listed with values (xs 12 to 7xl 82; none 100%, tight 105%, snug 126%, normal 150%, relaxed 160%). On a bound field Detach is the first item, and hovering the field shows the token name, such as text-lg.
  4. For dimensions, the W and H dropdowns list Spacing and Container tokens below Fixed, Fit, Fill and Relative. Gap, padding, radius, letter spacing and border color take tokens too.
  5. To dim a color without another color token, click the fill’s percentage field and choose an opacity token; the September demo paired ink with muted at 60%.
Shown at 2:13

Update and rename tokens from hand edits (set_tokens)

  1. Before editing, ask the agent which layers use a token: find_nodes accepts a token name as its style value. In an August 2026 demo a search for #000000 also matched 0-valued properties, and the agent read the icon subtrees separately to catch SVG stroke colors.
  2. Detach the elements you want to explore and try values in the color picker (sRGB or Display P3 tabs, with L C H, H S L and R G B rows).
  3. Prompt with the frame and the tokens: look at the first onboarding frame, grab the new colors for accent and gold label, update those tokens, and rename them.
  4. The agent read #89F0C5 and #319F77 and called set_tokens once: --color-accent became --color-teal and --color-gold became --color-teal-deep, and var() references followed the rename. Entry shape: {"name": "--color-accent", "newName": "--color-teal", "value": "#89F0C5"}; "delete": true removes a token.
  5. Re-link the elements you detached: they kept literal values and will not follow the next edit.
  6. Review neighbors: --color-gold-deep kept a stale name, and the new teal sat close to the success green.
  7. To carry the result back to code, ask for get_tokens with format tailwind (an @theme block) or css (a :root block), filtered with namePattern such as --color-* if needed.
Shown at 7:31

Copy a file’s tokens to another file

  1. In the source file, click the Paper logo at the top left, hover Theme and choose Copy theme.
  2. Open or create the destination file. In a file without tokens, Copy theme and Clear theme are grayed out and the Fill row has no token button.
  3. Choose Paper logo › Theme › Paste theme. A Theme pasted toast confirms, and the token button now lists the same tokens.
  4. Treat the copy as independent: copy again after changing the source, or ask an agent to compare get_tokens output across the two files and create or update what differs. Clear theme, and pasting into a file that already has tokens, were not demonstrated.
Shown at 0:10

Set an exact variable font weight

  1. Select a text layer set in a font with variable axes (DM Sans in the demo).
  2. Click the more button (sliders icon) at the top right of the Text section, then the Variable font tab; the other tabs are Formatting and Features.
  3. Drag Weight or type a value: 400 is Regular, 100 is thin, 800 is extra bold, and values between the stops, such as 364 or 560, work too. The weight dropdown’s label follows the value.
  4. Leave Automatic optical sizing checked unless you need a fixed Optical size; the Optical size field stays grayed while it is on.
  5. Record any custom weight, for example as a font weight token, so the implemented product uses the same number.

Limits and what is coming

  • Modes (light and dark, possibly contrast) and theme classes (bundled styles such as an H1, or a card’s shadows, borders and radius) were announced but not shipped as of September 2026. light-dark() values import as their light value, so a dark variant needs dark tokens applied to a duplicated frame.
  • Tokens belong to one file. Copy theme and Paste theme make an independent copy; linked libraries were still in progress as of September 2026.
  • On token-bound text written by agents, the font weight field has read Unavailable (a June 2026 viewer report and a September 2026 demo). Check weights after an agent pass.
  • In a June 2026 demo, line-height tokens came out as percentages (100% to 160%) although the brief asked for px. Paper’s agent guide (October 2026) prefers px for --leading-* tokens and em for --tracking-* tokens.

Build it in Paper

  1. Open the target file in Paper Desktop and ask your agent: “Create tokens in the open Paper file based on the CSS variables in this codebase.” Accept the import when its summary lists counts per category, source files and how light-dark() values and aliases were handled. Without a codebase, create the roles by hand in the Theme tab with +.
  2. Build a specimen frame with page background, surface, primary and secondary text, boundary, action and selected state. Apply colors with the four-circle Color tokens button beside each Fill, sizes and line heights from the Text section’s dropdowns, and spacing or radius from their fields.
  3. Select a specimen text layer and confirm that size and line height sit in small boxes, which marks a bound token; hover a box to read its name, such as text-lg, and check Selection colors for stray hex values.
  4. Change one token in the Theme tab: click it, edit Value, compare Previous and New in the color picker, then close the editor to save. Inspect the specimen and one representative screen for the expected changes and nothing else.
  5. If another file needs the set, choose Paper logo › Theme › Copy theme, then Paste theme in the destination, and record which file is the source, because the copy does not stay linked.

Check before you move on

  • Does every color, size, radius and spacing value on the frame come from a token, or does Selection colors still list stray hex values?
  • Does each token name describe a role (surface, action, danger) rather than a hue, and would a rename leave a related token with a stale name?
  • If you edit the action token now, which layers should change, and is anything detached that will not follow?
  • Do the type tokens give clear steps between title, heading, body and label at the sizes you actually use?
  • If other files use this system, which file is the source, and when was its theme last copied?

Common mistakes

Detaching a token to try a color, then leaving the literal value in place.

Once you decide, update the token in the Theme tab or with set_tokens and re-link the detached layers; Selection colors shows any hex values left behind.

Letting an agent create tokens on every request, or create semantic aliases before the palette they point at.

Ask it to run get_tokens first, state whether it may create or rename tokens, and have it create palette tokens before aliases.

Picking dark-mode colors by eye, or recoloring the light frame itself.

Duplicate the frame and ask the agent to apply the file’s dark tokens or the codebase’s dark-mode variables to the copy, as two 2026 demos did, leaving the light frame unchanged.

Treating magic swatches as tokens.

They are plain layers named Color #HEX. Apply the colors you keep to a fill and save them with + in the token menu, or create them with create_tokens.

Chapter 06Part 2 · Visual language

Make information easy to judge

A useful chart or dashboard helps the reader answer a specific question without hiding the source, unit or uncertainty behind its visual polish.

Start from the question and the content

A number becomes useful when the reader knows what it measures, which period it covers and what to compare it with. “Higher” has no clear meaning without a reference. Before choosing a chart, write the decision in an ordinary sentence: compare a scenario with its baseline, find the item leading a ranking, or identify an item below its target. The sentence reveals the relationships the display must preserve.

Realistic content changes design choices. Long category names need room. Different units need separation. Missing observations need an honest state. Paper’s Notion demonstration is relevant because an agent reads a named page through an MCP connection and lays it out as editable layers before any refinement. That is a transfer of material for a design, not evidence that the canvas has become a continuously updating database view: when the source changes, you ask again.

The chart should reveal a relationship, while its labels preserve the exact meaning.

The principle of chapter 6

Study 06 · change it yourself
Interactive study: Information. It runs in the web edition with JavaScript.

Choose an encoding that supports comparison

For values that must be compared precisely, position on a shared scale is a strong starting point. An aligned bar or dot can reveal an ordering faster than differently sized cards containing large numbers. The number remains useful as a label; the chart supplies the relationship. In Paper a bar is an ordinary frame or SVG shape, so the scale is something you set deliberately: one ratio from value to width, applied to every row.

Use a consistent scale when neighboring panels invite direct comparison. If one panel silently changes its range, identical bar lengths can represent different values. A target marker should look different from an observed amount. An uncertainty interval should look different from a decorative background band. The reader should be able to distinguish measurement, reference and qualification without memorizing an elaborate legend.

Color should carry a limited, stable responsibility. It can distinguish a scenario from a baseline or mark the selected series, but adding a unique color to every label often creates more decoding work. A mostly neutral field makes selective emphasis easier to read. Paper’s agent guide (October 2026) makes the same argument: one intense color moment is stronger than five, and secondary colors are meant for cases such as categories, complex data visualization and success, warning or error states. Store series colors as tokens so every chart keeps the same meanings.

Keep the caveat next to the claim

A synthetic example can teach a chart without pretending to be a result. Label it where the values are read, not only in a distant footer. Likewise, a conditional estimate needs its condition near the conclusion. The visual design should make the limitation part of the reading experience rather than a small-print correction to an overconfident headline.

Review the labels with the chart hidden, then the chart with its explanatory paragraph hidden; in Paper, Show / hide (⇧⌘H) on each group makes this a quick test. Each should contribute something useful. When an agent builds the chart, ask for the review Paper already expects of agents: a screenshot after each section with a verdict on spacing, typography, contrast and alignment. Add two questions of your own: is the scale shared, and does every caveat sit next to its number?

In Paper

How it works in Paper

As of September 2026, no Paper video or doc shows a chart component or live data binding: a chart or table is ordinary frames, text and SVG, which map to HTML with flexbox. Real content arrives through an agent that reads another source (an MCP server such as Notion, a repository’s API, a web search) and writes layers with write_html as a one-time copy, or through Paper Snapshot captures. Paper’s agent rules exclude HTML tables and CSS grid, require fixed-width lanes, and allow tokens in SVG fills and strokes.

Checked against the videos and documentation as of September 2026. Paper ships often; the release timeline in the reference shows what changed when.

Pull a named page from another MCP source and design it

  1. Add the source’s MCP server to your agent. The demo pasted the command from Notion’s docs into the terminal, claude mcp add --transport http notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp, then launched claude; the Paper MCP was already installed.
  2. Type /mcp to check both servers. Notion showed Status connected, Auth authenticated and 12 tools; a first connection goes through Notion’s OAuth flow in the browser.
  3. Name the content and the goal in one prompt: “grab our core Values page from Notion and create a nice design in Paper to highlight the content.” Approve tool permissions when asked.
  4. Expect parallel reads (notion-search next to Paper’s get_basic_info), then notion-fetch, get_font_family_info, a written design brief, create_artboard and a series of write_html calls with named layers.
  5. Refine by hand. The layers are a copy of the page at that moment, so rerun the prompt when the source changes.
Shown at 0:41

Fill a layout with real records from a repository or a live page

  1. Run the agent inside the repository that owns the data, with the Paper file open.
  2. Name the frame and the source together: “In Paper, please build out this ‘for you’ section … use the data from the API in this repo.” The demo agent duplicated an existing card and filled the copies with real playlist names.
  3. Watch the canvas: the agent’s avatar joins yours, and dotted markers show which frames it is reading.
  4. To see the result in context, capture the live page with Paper Snapshot (⌘Return grabs the whole page), paste it, and paste the new section inside it; untick Absolute position so the section joins the page’s flex flow.
  5. Ask for alternatives on a duplicate (“duplicate this frame and show me …”) so the original stays intact.
⌘Return
Shown at 2:16

Build a table or bar chart from flex rows

  1. Select a label and a bar rectangle and press ⇧A (Wrap in flex, in the Layout section) to make one row; set the gap in the Flex section.
  2. Give each column a fixed-width slot: set the label’s W to Fixed so every row shares the same lane. Paper’s agent guide asks agents for width plus flexShrink: 0, even where a row leaves the slot empty, and warns that gap alone does not align columns.
  3. Set the track that holds the bar to Fill (⌥ + double-click its edge) and the row’s height to Fit (double-click its top or bottom edge).
  4. Duplicate the row for each item, then select the rows and press ⇧A again to wrap them in a flex frame; set its direction to vertical in the Flex section if needed.
  5. With an agent, ask for flex rows with inline styles and inline SVG marks colored with var() tokens; the write_html rules exclude <table>, display: grid, margin and display: inline.
⇧A⌥Double-clickDouble-click
Shown at 1:36

Check scales, lanes and overflow

  1. Select a bar and read W in the Layout section; every bar should equal its value times the same scale factor.
  2. Hold ⌥ with a layer selected to see its distances to the surrounding edges, and confirm that every bar starts at the same zero point.
  3. Turn off Clip content (⌥C) on the parent to reveal labels or legend items that overflow; Wrap in the flex settings lets a legend row break onto new lines.
  4. After three or more rows, take a screenshot and trace vertical lines through labels, values and icons.
  5. For exact numbers, ask the agent for get_computed_styles rather than reading a screenshot; Paper’s guide keeps screenshots for verification.
⌥⌥C
Shown at 12:00

Brief an agent from reference charts and real constraints

  1. Paste reference images next to the work (⌘V) and prompt: “look at the reference images & list best practices.” Edit the list before relying on it.
  2. Name the question the chart answers, the real values or their source, the units, and any caveat that must sit next to a number.
  3. Ask for the file’s tokens through var() for series colors and for layers named by meaning, like Header, Tactics Section and Footer in the Notion demo.
  4. Ask for a checkpoint screenshot after each section with a one-line verdict on spacing, typography, contrast and alignment, as the Notion demo’s agent produced.
  5. Copy a link to the target frame (⌘L) and paste it into follow-up prompts so the agent edits the right frame.
⌘V⌘L

ControlWhereWhat it does

Limits and what is coming

  • No chart component, data binding or live sync appears in Paper’s videos or docs as of September 2026; agent-written content is a one-time copy that you refresh by prompting again.
  • Paper’s agent rules (October 2026) exclude <table>, display: grid, margin and display: inline in write_html. Full CSS Grid authoring was planned, not shipped, as of September 2026, although grid elements gained alignment and gap controls that month.
  • Rich text inside one text layer, such as a bold number with a regular unit, was announced as coming soon in September 2026; until then, use separate text layers in a flex row.
  • The Heatmap shader is a glow effect for images and shapes, listed with logo animations in Paper’s shader gallery; it does not plot data.
