Build it in Paper

  1. Bring real content in first: connect the source through its MCP server, a repository’s API or a capture of the live page, and ask the agent to place the actual labels and values on a new artboard. Mark any invented values as such inside the frame.
  2. Build one comparison row: select a label and a bar, press ⇧A (Wrap in flex), give the label a Fixed width so every row shares the same lane, and set the bar’s track to Fill with ⌥ + double-click on its edge.
  3. Duplicate the row (⌘D) for each item and set each bar’s W from one shared scale. Put units in the labels, and draw the target as a distinct mark, such as a thin line with Absolute position checked.
  4. Keep an unavailable observation in its lane with an explicit “No data” label. Hold ⌥ to check distances, turn off Clip content (⌥C) to reveal overflowing labels, and take a screenshot after three rows.
  5. Hide the chart group with Show / hide (⇧⌘H) and read the labels alone, then show it again and hide the explanatory text.

Check before you move on

  • Can you state the question the chart answers in one sentence, and does the layout answer it first?
  • Do all comparable marks share one scale and one zero point, and does the target look different from an observed value?
  • Are the real labels readable at their longest with Clip content off, and does a missing value keep its lane?
  • Is every unit, source and caveat next to the number it qualifies rather than in a footer?
  • Does a vertical line traced through labels, values and icons stay straight across every row?

Common mistakes

Designing the chart with placeholder labels and round numbers, then finding that real names wrap and real values crowd the scale.

Bring real content in first through an MCP source, a repository’s API or a capture, and label any invented values inside the frame.

Aligning table columns with gap alone, so values drift when a label or icon changes width.

Give every column a fixed-width slot (W Fixed; width plus flexShrink: 0 in agent HTML), even where a row has no content, and screenshot after three rows.

Asking an agent for an HTML table or a CSS grid.

Ask for flex rows with inline styles and inline SVG marks; Paper’s write_html rules exclude <table> and display: grid.

Treating the canvas as a live view of the source.

Write the source and the retrieval date on the frame, and rerun the prompt when the data changes; as of September 2026 Paper does not refresh it.

Chapter 07Part 2 · Visual language

Finish the asset at the size people will see

An editable vector is a starting material. Its quality depends on silhouette, stroke, bounds and the way it participates in the composition.

An illustration has a job

A useful asset contributes something the surrounding layout cannot say as efficiently. An icon can identify a familiar action; a diagram can reveal a relationship; an illustration can establish a tone. Decide that job before choosing how to make the asset. A decorative asset placed beside every paragraph can increase visual activity without increasing understanding.

For an interface icon, recognition at the final small size matters more than impressive detail when enlarged. For a cover illustration, composition and negative space may matter more than exact geometry. These different jobs imply different finishing decisions. The same intricate drawing that works on a chapter opener may become an indistinct mark beside a compact label.

An asset is finished when it serves the composition at its actual display size.

The principle of chapter 7

Study 07 · change it yourself
Interactive study: Vector. It runs in the web edition with JavaScript.

Treat generated geometry as editable material

Paper’s Quiver tutorial demonstrates a complete idea: describe the subject, style, colors and restraint, generate an SVG, then refine it by hand. The presenter hides three unwanted polygons, sets two mismatched stroke widths (0.28 and 0.99) to 1, deletes a stray path, trims sections of another and skips about five more minutes of editing. The useful distinction is between requesting a plausible starting image and accepting a finished asset. Generation solves the first problem; design judgment still solves the second.

An SVG contains shapes that can be inspected independently. In Paper, an SVG layer is a container that behaves like a frame and clips what it holds; the Path layers inside it are the editable geometry, each with its own fill and stroke. A click selects the container, a double-click selects one path, and a second double-click shows that path’s nodes. Moving a point is not the same as moving the asset. After an edit, inspect the container’s bounds: a node dragged past them is cut off at the edge.

Look at the silhouette before the details. A good small asset should remain recognizable when its internal decoration is temporarily ignored. Then inspect stroke consistency and the spaces between shapes. A cramped gap may close when the image is reduced; a thin stroke may disappear against the intended background. Generated output makes this check necessary: the tutorial’s illustration arrived as 3 polygons and about 20 separate paths with uneven strokes. The final composition, rather than the enlarged editing view, is the meaningful test.

Keep the asset and the layout independent

Use a vector for geometry that benefits from remaining editable, such as a logo or an icon. Keep ordinary interface text as text and structural regions as frames. Flattening the entire screen into an image can preserve its current appearance while discarding the relationships needed for later edits, accessibility and implementation. Choose the representation according to what must remain changeable.

In Paper, the container is the asset’s boundary. Containers that Paper creates, whether you draw with the pen or generate with Create SVG, start at 256 × 256 with Clip content on, which is rarely the size the asset will be seen at. With a path selected, dragging the container’s edges changes only the bounds, so you can tighten them around the artwork or give a clipped node room; the paths keep their size. As of September 2026, true crop, scale and resize for SVGs, boolean operations and snapping to other geometry were still roadmap items, so judge placement by eye at the real size, on the real background. The best edit often removes a distraction instead of adding another effect.

In Paper

How it works in Paper

As of September 2026, Paper edits SVGs on the canvas, a beta since June 2026. An SVG layer is a clipping container, 256 × 256 when Paper creates it, holding Path layers with their own Fill and Stroke (width, Above fill or Below fill). A double-click reaches a path and a second one its nodes; the pen tool (P) draws new paths. Create SVG (⇧⌘J) generates editable vectors with QuiverAI models, and right-click › Vectorize image converts a raster. Booleans, snapping to other geometry and true SVG scaling remain on the roadmap.

Checked against the videos and documentation as of September 2026. Paper ships often; the release timeline in the reference shows what changed when.

Edit a path inside an SVG

  1. Click the SVG on the canvas to select its container.
  2. Double-click to select one of its paths, or pick the Path in the layers list. Drag its handles to move, resize or rotate that path alone; the other paths stay put.
  3. Double-click the selected path to enter vector editing mode, then drag its nodes. Paper’s vector documentation also lists Enter for this step.
  4. Recolor the path in the right panel’s Fill row. Click + beside Stroke to add a stroke, then set its color and width.
  5. Leave vector editing with Escape or a double-click on empty canvas.
Double-clickEsc
Shown at 2:04

Draw a shape with the pen tool

  1. Press P, or click the pen button in the toolbar, just below the rectangle tool.
  2. Click to place points. Points snap to the nearest half pixel; hold Shift while clicking to place the next point at a 45° angle.
  3. Click the first point to close the shape.
  4. A new pen path has no fill and a 1 px stroke in 000000, Above fill. Click + beside Fill to add a fill, and – beside Stroke to remove the stroke if you want a solid shape.
P⇧Click
Shown at 3:11

Shape curves and add points

  1. Enter vector editing with the move tool active (the arrow at the top of the toolbar), not the pen, so clicks move nodes instead of adding them.
  2. Hold ⌘ and drag from a node to pull out curve handles. Once the segment curves you can release ⌘; the two handles stay mirrored.
  3. Hold ⌥ while dragging a handle to move it on its own. Hold ⌘ again to mirror the pair once more.
  4. Hold ⌘ and drag from the middle of a straight segment to bow it into a curve, with handles at both ends.
  5. To insert a point, switch to the pen tool, hover anywhere on the edge and click.
⌘Drag⌥Drag
Shown at 4:02

Add paths to the right SVG

  1. To extend the path you are editing, draw with the pen while it is in vector editing mode; the new segments join that same Path layer.
  2. To add a separate path, press Escape to leave vector editing, keep the SVG or one of its paths selected, and draw with the pen inside the container. A new Path appears in that SVG with its own fill and stroke, and moves independently.
  3. Drawing outside the container’s bounding box creates a new SVG container around the new path.
  4. To bring that path into the original SVG, select it and press ⌘C, select the original SVG and press ⌘V. The copy lands inside the original; the stray container remains until you delete it.
⌘C⌘V
Shown at 5:14

Generate an SVG with Create SVG

  1. Click Create SVG in the toolbar (a frame icon with a sparkle, below Create image) or press ⇧⌘J. A prompt panel opens at the bottom of the canvas.
  2. Pick a model. In June 2026 the menu offered QuiverAI Arrow 1.1 (“Balanced SVG quality and speed”, the default) and QuiverAI Arrow 1.1 Max (“For detailed SVGs, takes more time”).
  3. Write the prompt: the subject, the drawing style (line quality, and whether it is an illustration, an icon or a logo), specific colors, and restraint such as minimal with lots of negative space.
  4. Click Create SVG. A placeholder layer named “Generating with QuiverAI…” appears and the drawing builds live on the canvas.
  5. The result is an SVG layer named from the prompt, 256 × 256 with Clip content on. With it selected, the panel shows a row with its thumbnail and prompt. Run a cleanup pass before using it.
⇧⌘J
Shown at 0:11

Clean up a generated SVG

  1. Expand the SVG in the layers list and take inventory; the tutorial’s result held 3 Polygon layers and about 20 Path layers.
  2. Hide unwanted shapes with the eye toggle before deciding to delete them.
  3. Select paths one at a time and read their Stroke width. Set lines that should match to one value; in the tutorial a 0.28 stroke and a 0.99 stroke both became 1.
  4. Select a stray path and delete it. Each stroke is its own path, so the rest of the drawing holds together.
  5. For a path that is only partly wrong, enter vector editing, drag the doubtful piece aside to see what it is, then select its nodes and press Delete. ⌘Z restores anything removed by mistake.
  6. Judge the result at display size before calling it finished.
Delete⌘Z

Build it in Paper

  1. Create or import an SVG with a defined role and display size: paste one (⌘V), draw with the pen tool (P) or generate one with Create SVG (⇧⌘J). Duplicate it (⌘D) and keep the untouched copy beside the working version.
  2. Expand the SVG in the layers list and take inventory of its Path and Polygon layers; hide doubtful parts with the eye toggle before deleting anything.
  3. Double-click into a path and again into its nodes. Match stroke widths in the Stroke row, choose Above fill or Below fill deliberately, delete stray paths, and press Escape to leave vector editing.
  4. With a path selected, drag the container’s edges until the bounds fit the artwork and nothing important is clipped.
  5. Place the asset at its real size on its real background, view it at 100% zoom (the zoom level shows at the top of the right panel), and compare its silhouette with the untouched copy.

Check before you move on

  • Does the asset still read at its display size when you ignore interior detail and look only at the silhouette?
  • Do strokes meant to match share one width value, and is each stroke’s position (Above fill or Below fill) a deliberate choice?
  • Is anything cut off by the SVG container, or is empty container space throwing off alignment with its neighbors?
  • Has every hidden or stray path been either restored for a reason or deleted?
  • Is interface text still live text, with only icons, logos and illustrations drawn as vectors?

Common mistakes

Dragging a node past the SVG’s edge and concluding the shape is broken when it is only clipped.

Select a path and drag the container’s edge outward until the shape shows, or keep the node inside; Clip content is on by default.

Drawing a new shape outside the container and ending up with a second SVG.

Select the SVG or one of its paths first and draw inside its bounds. To merge a stray, copy its path (⌘C), select the original SVG and paste (⌘V).

Entering vector editing with the pen tool active and adding points by accident.

Switch to the move tool before you double-click into the path; use the pen only when you mean to add points.

Accepting a generated SVG as finished because it looks good enlarged.

Inventory its layers, hide extras, match stroke widths, delete strays, then judge it at display size against an untouched copy.

Where a design starts (a live site, a Figma file, generated images) and how effects such as shaders earn their place.

Chapter 08Part 3 · Material

Choose the right starting material

Snapshot, Figma paste, HTML import and image generation begin with different kinds of evidence and preserve different kinds of editability.

Capture the product you intend to change

Starting from the actual interface gives a redesign useful resistance. Its current content, spacing and awkward cases are already present, so the proposal must respond to a real situation. Record the viewport and the state being captured. A populated results screen and an empty state are different design problems even if they share the same route.

Paper Snapshot is a Chrome extension that captures the part of a page you choose: hover until a blue box surrounds it, fine-tune the target with the arrow keys, press Return (or ⌘Return for the whole page), then paste into Paper with ⌘V. Because the page and Paper’s canvas are both HTML and CSS, the capture arrives as editable layers rather than a screenshot: text layers, flex frames with their gaps and Fill or Fit sizing, per-side borders with alpha, radii, and every color listed in Selection colors. It is a visual and structural starting point, fixed at the size and state you captured. It does not carry the application’s authentication, persistence or live data behavior into the canvas; those responsibilities stay in the running product.

Capture preserves a starting point; import translates structure; generation creates new material.

The principle of chapter 8

Study 08 · change it yourself
Interactive study: Starting material. It runs in the web edition with JavaScript.

Distinguish import from invention

Normal copy and paste moves a Figma selection into Paper: ⌘C in Figma, ⌘V in Paper. Frames keep their names, sizes and structure, and images follow once you connect a Figma account that can open the file. Components, instances and variables arrive detached, masks are hidden, and effects with no CSS equivalent, such as noise, glass or gradient strokes, do not come across. HTML paste has a different boundary: only inline styles transfer, and class names and stylesheet rules are discarded. The important question is therefore not whether an import succeeded, but which decisions survived in an editable form and which now need to be restated.

An image has a different role. A screenshot is useful evidence of appearance, but its pixels do not explain the original layout hierarchy. A generated image is new material produced from a brief, rather than a record of the existing product. Place these materials on the canvas with clear purposes: reference, editable baseline, or proposed asset. Confusing those purposes makes a visually convincing file harder to trust.

Image generation benefits from a concrete composition brief: subject, materials, surface, light, palette, aspect ratio and the space reserved for nearby copy. In Paper, Create image (⇧⌘I) sends that brief to the model you pick, and selecting the result makes it context, so the next prompt changes one thing while the rest of the scene holds. This is a production method rather than a promise about a particular model’s accuracy: in Paper’s own demo, a lighting change also removed a wall. If the result must describe a real place, person or product, verify it against appropriate evidence instead of accepting plausible detail as fact.

Inspect the transfer before redesigning it

A missing image can make a captured layout look cleaner while actually making it incomplete. A substituted font can change every line break. Compare the imported baseline with the source before you start improving it, so translation errors do not become mistaken design decisions. When a capture from a local development server arrives without its images, the usual cause is cross-origin blocking. Paper’s troubleshooting page says to allow the origin https://app.paper.design in the server’s CORS settings and, on Vite 6 and later, which blocks /@fs/ paths regardless of CORS, to serve assets from public/.

Keep the three kinds of material apart on the canvas. Leave the original capture untouched and duplicate it (⌘D) for the working version. Rename generic layers: Snapshot names its frames Frame, and Figma pastes keep names such as Property 1=Variant4. Generated images are named from their prompt, and their Image fill records the model and the pixel size, which tells you whether the resolution suits the display size. Then explain each intentional difference. That creates a clear line from the product you observed to the proposal you want implemented.

In Paper

How it works in Paper

As of September 2026, Paper takes starting material five ways. Paper Snapshot, a Chrome extension, rebuilds a page region or a whole page as editable HTML/CSS layers. Figma selections paste with ⌘C and ⌘V, components detached. HTML pastes with inline styles only. Create image (⇧⌘I) generates images from a choice of models, and since September agents can generate through the MCP. Plain images paste too, and right-click offers Remove background, Vectorize image and Extract colors. Captured flex, borders and radii arrive as real CSS properties, not pixels.

Checked against the videos and documentation as of September 2026. Paper ships often; the release timeline in the reference shows what changed when.

Install and start Paper Snapshot

  1. Open the Paper Snapshot page in the Chrome Web Store (linked from Paper’s site) and click Add to Chrome.
  2. Pin it: open Chrome’s Extensions menu, find Paper Snapshot and click its pin so the icon stays in the toolbar.
  3. On the page you want, click the Paper Snapshot icon. If Chrome’s Extensions menu lists it under Access requested, click it there to give it access to that site.
  4. A hint bar appears at the top of the page: Click or ↵ to capture, ↑ ↓ to fine-tune target, Esc to cancel. In the June and September 2026 recordings it also shows ⌘ ↵ to capture page.
  5. Paper’s quick start page adds ⇧⌘P to switch the extension on; you can remap it at chrome://extensions/shortcuts.
Shown at 0:34

Capture a region or a whole page

  1. Hover the page. A blue box marks the element under the pointer; everything inside it is the selection.
  2. Press ↑ to widen the target to an enclosing element. The hint bar pairs it with ↓ for the other direction.
  3. Click or press Return to capture the target, or press ⌘Return to capture the entire page. A Capturing selection… badge shows progress, then a toast confirms “Copied to clipboard. Ready to paste into Paper.”
  4. Switch to Paper, on the web or in the desktop app, and press ⌘V on the canvas.
  5. Press Esc instead to cancel without capturing.
↑Return⌘Return⌘VEsc
Shown at 1:02

Paste a Figma selection

  1. In Figma, select frames or layers (⌘A selects everything on the page) and press ⌘C.
  2. In Paper, press ⌘V. A toast reads “Pasting from Figma. Images will be fetched.”
  3. If the selection holds images, the Images from Figma dialog appears the first time. Choose Connect and continue, approve Paper on the Figma page that opens in your browser, then return to Paper. Continue without images pastes the layers without them.
  4. Check the result against Figma: frames keep their names and sizes (two 1000 × 700 frames named Property 1=Variant4 and Property 1=Variant5 in the demo), nested frames carry flex settings with Fill and Fit sizing, and components arrive detached.
  5. If images are missing, connect an account that can open the Figma file; Figma’s API rate limits can also hold them back.
⌘C⌘V
Shown at 0:39

Generate and iterate an image

  1. Click Create image in the toolbar (a picture icon with a sparkle) or press ⇧⌘I. A prompt panel opens at the bottom of the canvas.
  2. Pick a model. The default, Variety pack, sends one prompt to four models and returns four images.
  3. Pick an aspect ratio: Square 1:1 (the default); Landscape 3:2, 4:3, 16:9 or 2:1; Portrait 2:3, 3:4, 9:16 or 1:2.
  4. Describe subject, materials, surface, light, mood and photographic register, then click Create image. A placeholder layer (Generating with Grok, in the demo) becomes an image layer named from the prompt.
  5. To iterate, select the image. The panel shows it as context, with its thumbnail and original prompt, and hides the ratio menu. Ask for one change and keep the same model.
  6. Each version lands beside the source at the same size. Reselect the original before the next change, and click away to drop the context.
⇧⌘I
Shown at 0:08

Cut out a subject

  1. Right-click the image on the canvas.
  2. Choose Remove background, in the menu’s image section beside Vectorize image, Extract colors and Open image in new tab.
  3. Wait a couple of seconds. The subject now sits on transparency, and the layer keeps its original size (1731 × 2181 in the demo).
  4. Place the cutout in its target frame, which crops it at its edges. To trim the transparent margin, hold ⌘ while dragging a resize handle; that crops the image instead of scaling it.
Right-click⌘Drag
Shown at 0:06

Generate images through an agent

  1. Connect the agent once: with nothing selected, click Connect your agent in the right panel’s MCP section, choose the harness and click its Add to button (for example Add to Cursor), or open Or, install manually.
  2. Ask in plain words and say where the images go. One of the dialog’s test prompts is “Generate an image of a beautiful sunset in Paper”.
  3. In the September 2026 demo, asking for the variety pack of models produced a board titled with the subject and four images captioned by model: OpenAI Image 2.5, Nano Banana 2, Flux 2 Pro and Recraft V4.1.
  4. Behind the scenes the agent writes paper-gen:// image URLs naming a model, a prompt and an optional aspect ratio. Each image costs 1 to 4 usage units depending on the model, and a call that authors more than 10 images is declined as a whole.
  5. Paper’s agent guide tells agents to generate only when you ask, and to make variants as new images that reference the original.

Limits and what is coming

  • Paper Snapshot is a Chrome extension; no other browser appears in the sources (Chrome Web Store version 0.4.4, updated 27 September 2026). A capture is a static copy at the width and state you captured, with generic layer names and none of the page’s behavior or live data.
  • Figma paste, in beta at its June 2026 launch, detaches components, instances and variables, hides masks, turns diamond gradients into radial ones, and does not support noise, texture, glass, repeat or symmetry effects, gradient strokes, arbitrary dash lengths, rich text or pass-through blending of backgrounds (Paper’s Figma paste documentation, October 2026).
  • HTML paste reads inline styles only and has no rich text: a block whose children are all inline becomes a single text layer, so mixed styling inside it is lost.
  • Image generation is metered. In May 2026 the panel warned “You are approaching your rate limit. New images are available each Saturday.” with an Upgrade button; Paper’s pricing lists limited generation on Free and 100 times more per week on Pro, and the MCP charges 1 to 4 usage units per image depending on the model.

Build it in Paper

  1. Open the live page at a known width and state, click the Paper Snapshot icon in Chrome’s toolbar, hover the region, refine it with ↑ and ↓, and press Return; press ⌘Return instead to capture the whole page.
  2. In Paper, press ⌘V. Compare text, images, fonts and spacing with the live page, rename the generic Frame layers, and duplicate the capture (⌘D) before editing.
  3. For Figma material, copy in Figma (⌘C), paste in Paper (⌘V) and choose Connect and continue when Images from Figma appears, then look for detached components. For HTML, inline the styles before you copy.
  4. Generate new imagery with Create image (⇧⌘I): pick a model and an aspect ratio, select the result to change one thing per prompt, and use right-click › Remove background for cutouts.
  5. Group captured references, editable baselines and generated assets in separately labeled areas so no one mistakes one for another.

Check before you move on

  • Did you record the URL, viewport width and state you captured, and does the pasted frame match the live page’s text, images and fonts?
  • Have captured and pasted layers been renamed from Frame or Figma variant names to names that say what they are?
  • Which parts are reference, which are editable baseline and which are generated proposals, and is each labeled that way on the canvas?
  • Did any image fail to transfer, or any component arrive detached, and have you restated those decisions?
  • For each generated image, is the source resolution in its Image fill enough for its display size, and did any edit change something you did not ask for?

Common mistakes

Redesigning directly on the only capture of the live page.

Duplicate it with ⌘D and keep the original untouched beside the working copy, so every change can be compared with what shipped.

Pasting HTML that relies on a stylesheet and getting unstyled layers.

Inline the styles as style attributes before copying; Paper’s HTML paste discards class names and selectors.

Asking an image model for several changes at once and losing the parts that worked.

Select the original as context, request one change per prompt with the same model, and compare each version with the source.

Accepting a Snapshot of a local development site that came in without its images.

Allow https://app.paper.design in the dev server’s CORS settings (on Vite 6 and later, serve assets from public/), then capture again.

Chapter 09Part 3 · Material

Shaders: give effects a precise visual purpose

A shader can create material, light or motion. It becomes useful design when its role is clear and the surrounding content remains readable.

Choose the role before the preset

An effect can establish atmosphere, make a brand mark distinctive or create a focal point. Those are different jobs from explaining a value or completing an action. Begin by naming the job. If a static texture supplies enough character, movement may add distraction without adding meaning, and in Paper every animated shader becomes a still at Speed 0%. The strongest effect is often the one whose intensity has been reduced to fit the composition.

Paper’s Shaders panel sorts its shaders into three families, and the family matters more than any slider. Image filters, such as Fluted Glass, Halftone CMYK and Lens Distortion, transform an image you feed them. Logo animations (Heatmap, Liquid Metal and Gem Smoke) react to the edges of a shape you supply. Effects, from Mesh Gradient to God Rays, generate a field from parameters alone. As of September 2026 that is 7 image filters, 3 logo animations and 20 effects. Choosing between these families is more consequential than moving several sliders on an unsuitable preset.

An effect should support one visual purpose without borrowing attention from the task.

The principle of chapter 9

Study 09 · change it yourself
Interactive study: Shaders. It runs in the web edition with JavaScript.

Tune the relationship, not the isolated preview

Paper’s logo-animation tutorial captures a real site footer with Paper Snapshot, places a Gem Smoke version of the brand’s wordmark inside it and tunes the smoke beside the footer’s links. That is the decisive move. A dramatic mark in an empty preview can become distracting on a real page. Assess the amount of motion, the brightness of the busiest region and the contrast of nearby text together, because they compete for the same attention. In that demo the fixes were concrete: Outer glow at 0% so no smoke crossed the links, less Inner glow, and Clip content on the frame so the smoke stopped at its edge.

Change one parameter family at a time: first the input and its fit, then the palette, then the form (shape, proportion, distortion, contour), and only then motion and surface detail such as Speed and grain. Paper’s own rebuild of a reference follows this order: nearest preset, then colors sampled from the reference, then Speed, Scale, Softness and swirl. Each change has a visible cause. If several controls move together, an attractive result is hard to reproduce or refine. A habit from the same tutorials helps: push a slider to its extreme to see its range, then settle.

Some controls depend on others. The Lens Distortion reference makes Spread the master control of its color split: at 0, the other color controls do nothing. Waves’ frequency needs some amplitude, and Halftone Dots loses the image entirely at zero Contrast. An apparently inactive slider may therefore be working as specified. Keep the selected effect’s parameter reference nearby, and save the settings with the input image and final dimensions. A preset without its context is only a partial description of the result.

Separate visual atmosphere from evidence

Names such as Heatmap, Waves or Voronoi describe aesthetic shader families, not data bindings. A heat-like color treatment does not become a measured intensity map because the name sounds scientific, and Voronoi cells are not real spatial partitions. Keep decorative effects outside charts and evidence-bearing text. Give the expressive material one bounded region, such as a cover, hero or footer band, and keep the information on a stable, opaque surface beside it.

Motion also needs a quiet version in the implemented product. The shader package pauses animation when a shader leaves the viewport or its tab is hidden, but it does not react to a reduced-motion preference on its own, so keep an accepted still (speed 0 at a chosen frame) and switch to it explicitly. Record the package version with the preset: in version 0.0.81 Paper Texture was rebuilt, its old folds became crumples, its old crumples became wrinkles, contrast and fade were removed, and old seeds no longer match visually. Recheck the composition after an upgrade, not only whether the code runs.

In Paper

How it works in Paper

As of September 2026, Paper’s Shaders panel (S) holds 30 shaders in three sections: 7 Image filters, 3 Logo animations and 20 Effects. Each shader is a layer with the usual Layout, Radius, Fill and Export panels, plus Presets, an Image or Shape input, Parameters and color lists. Animated shaders freeze at Speed 0%. Copy as React CSS gives a component from the open-source @paper-design/shaders-react package; @paper-design/shaders mounts the same shaders without React, as a canvas that fills its parent element.

Checked against the videos and documentation as of September 2026. Paper ships often; the release timeline in the reference shows what changed when.

Add a shader and tune it in order

  1. Press S, or click the last button in the left toolbar (a diamond in a square; builds before late May 2026 showed a cube icon).
  2. In the Shaders panel, click a tile under Image filters, Logo animations or Effects. The shader lands as its own layer named after the effect, usually at 800 × 600; resize it to its slot.
  3. Click through Presets and keep the closest. A preset rewrites every parameter, so choose it before tuning.
  4. Set colors next: click a swatch to open the picker (sRGB and Display P3 tabs, an eyedropper, OKLCH, HSL, RGB and hex fields) and remove extra colors with the minus button.
  5. Adjust Parameters one family at a time. Dragging a slider to its maximum shows the range before you settle.
  6. Set Speed last: lower it for calm motion, or set 0% for a still texture.
S
Shown at 0:32

Feed an image filter from the canvas and chain filters

  1. Add an image filter such as Fluted Glass. Its Image section shows a sample (flowers.webp, 1600×1200) with an eyedropper and a trash icon.
  2. Click the eyedropper (“Capture image from another element”), then click any layer: a photo, a generated image, a text layer or another shader. The input becomes a .webp named after that layer.
  3. Try the presets again on the new input, then lower Distortion or Size if the effect should be subtle.
  4. To chain, add a second filter, for example Halftone CMYK with the Vintage preset, and eyedrop the first shader. Its output arrives as “Fluted Glass.webp”.
Shown at 2:12

Animate a logo

  1. Press S and pick Heatmap, Liquid Metal or Gem Smoke under Logo animations. The default shape is a diamond.
  2. In Shape, click the eyedropper and then your logo layer, or click Choose file to upload one. Liquid Metal and Gem Smoke also have a dropdown of built-in shapes (Liquid Metal lists None, Circle, Daisy, Diamond and Metaballs).
  3. Set the shader’s Fill to the ground the logo sits on (black in the demos), or remove it when the page behind already provides that ground.
  4. Set Contour: 0% acts as a plain mask, low values react only at the rim, 100% fills the shape with edge-following bands.
  5. Lower the glows and Noise until the mark reads, then lower Speed. Next to text, set Outer glow to 0%.
S
Shown at 1:06

Put a shader inside a button or section

  1. Duplicate the component (⌘D) to keep a before and after. With nothing selected, set Page in the right panel to the product’s background so you judge the glow in context.
  2. Add the shader (Pulsing Border in the demo), remove its Fill and use the color list’s eyedropper (“Pick colors from another element”) on the original.
  3. Match the shape: Scale 100%, Roundness 100% for a pill, and Radius Full on the shader layer.
  4. Remove the component’s own fill, then drag the shader into the outer frame rather than the content frame.
  5. Because the frame uses flex, check Absolute position in Layout (under Wrap in flex), set W and H to Fill and X and Y to 0.
  6. For a hard inner edge, drag the shader above the opaque content frame in the layers list so it renders behind it. On a section, turn on Clip content (⌥C) so smoke or glow stops at the edge.
⌘D⌥C
Shown at 2:56

Freeze, copy or export a shader

  1. For a still, duplicate the shader and set Speed to 0% on the copy.
  2. Right-click and choose Copy as React CSS (⌥R), Copy as Tailwind (⌥T) or Copy as PNG. Since September 2026 the same options also sit behind the copy icon next to Export, where Copy as PNG shows ⇧⌘C.
  3. Paste the React code: it starts with the package and version (/** @paper-design/shaders-react@0.0.71 */ in March 2026), imports the component, links back to the Paper file and node, and passes each parameter as a prop.
  4. Read the props as the panel’s percentages divided by 100: Speed 350% becomes speed={3.5} and Scale 247% becomes scale={2.47}.
  5. For motion files, use the Video section (+) in the right panel; video export is a paid-plan feature.
⌥R⌥T⇧⌘C
Shown at 1:15

Use the shader in code

  1. Install the exact version named in the header, for example npm i @paper-design/shaders-react@0.0.81. Releases under 0.0.x can break, so pin it.
  2. Paste the component and give it a size with width and height or CSS; it renders a canvas that fills that box.
  3. Add a reduced-motion branch that renders the same props with speed 0 and a chosen frame. The package already pauses offscreen and in hidden tabs, but not for reduced motion.
  4. Without React, install @paper-design/shaders and call new ShaderMount(element, warpFragmentShader, uniforms, undefined, speed) with u_-prefixed uniforms; shaders that sample noise also need getShaderNoiseTexture().
  5. For large backgrounds, lower minPixelRatio (default 2) or maxPixelCount to cut GPU work; at speed 0 the animation loop stops, so a still costs nothing after its first frame.
Shown at 1:24

Inner glow / Outer glowRight panel › Parameters (Heatmap, Gem Smoke)Inner glow sizes the effect inside the shape’s bounds; Outer glow sizes it outside them.Set Outer glow to 0% when text sits next to the mark.
Color list (Foreground, Colors, Tint, Inner)Right panel, below ParametersThe shader’s palette. Click a swatch to edit it, + to add a color, minus to remove one; the list’s eyedropper (“Pick colors from another element”) samples colors from any layer, including images and other shaders.The label varies: Warp and Heatmap say Foreground, Gem Smoke says Colors and Inner, Liquid Metal says Tint.
Absolute positionRight panel › Layout, under Wrap in flex (children of a flex frame)Takes the shader out of the flex flow (CSS position: absolute) so it can sit behind content; Left and Top constraint menus and alignment buttons appear. Then set W and H to Fill and X and Y to 0.
Clip contentRight panel › the parent frame’s layout options (⌥C)Hides whatever extends past the frame, such as smoke or glow from a shader larger than its container.

Limits and what is coming

  • As of September 2026 the Paper MCP has no tool that inserts or edits a shader; presets, inputs and parameters are set by hand in the right panel.
  • Video export of shaders and frames is limited to paid (Pro) plans as of September 2026, according to Paper’s support shortcuts and build log.
  • Eyedropper captures are stored as .webp snapshots named after the source layer. No video shows them updating when the source changes, so re-capture after editing a source layer.
  • The shader library is Paper’s own: 30 shaders as of September 2026, extended through a monthly “shader of the month”. The roadmap lists more motion effects, image filters and post-processing effects as in progress, and particle systems, Three.js islands and Lottie or Rive embeds as planned, not shipped.

Understanding contour in Paper's logo animation shadersShort · 56 s · 9 July 2026

0:56

Contour at 18%, 0% and 100%

A recut of the Liquid Metal segment, on the Vercel triangle. Every pixel of a logo animation knows its distance to the shape’s edge, and Contour sets how far in that distance matters. At 18% only pixels near the rim react. At 0% nothing reacts to the edge, which looks like an ordinary shader masked by the shape. At 100% pixels deep inside follow the outline too, giving the strongest edge-following liquid bands. The full tutorial settles on 40%.

0:04Image filters: Lens Distortion0:06Presets and Image input0:12Focus, Swirl and Noise0:16Lens bulge -74%, Scale 140%0:20Five headline variants

Build it in Paper

  1. Place the image or logo you will treat beside an unchanged copy. Press S, pick the family that fits (an image filter for a picture, a logo animation for a mark, an effect for a generated field) and use the eyedropper in its Image or Shape section to capture your layer.
  2. Click the nearest preset first, then set colors with the color list’s eyedropper or typed values, then adjust one parameter family at a time, leaving Speed for last.
  3. Drag the shader into its frame, check Absolute position, set W and H to Fill and X and Y to 0, remove the shader’s Fill if the page should show through, and turn on Clip content (⌥C) on the parent.
  4. Watch the nearby text through a full cycle and lower Outer glow, Intensity or Speed until it stays legible. Duplicate the shader (⌘D) and set Speed to 0% on the copy for the still and reduced-motion state.
  5. Copy as React CSS (⌥R) and keep the header’s package version, the preset, the input image and the final size next to the shader.

Check before you move on

  • Can you name the one job this effect does, and would a still at Speed 0% do it as well?
  • Does every nearby line of text stay legible through a full animation cycle, at the size people will see it?
  • Is the shader absolutely positioned at Fill × Fill inside its frame, with Clip content on wherever smoke or glow could spill?
  • Have you saved the shader’s name, preset, parameter values, colors, input image, size and the package version from the Copy as React CSS header?
  • Is there a defined still frame for reduced motion, and does no decorative effect sit under a chart, number or form field?

Common mistakes

Tuning a shader, then clicking another preset to compare and losing every value.

Presets rewrite all parameters. Duplicate the shader first (⌘D) and try presets on the copy, or choose the preset before you tune.

Dropping a shader into a flex button or section, where it lines up beside the content instead of behind it.

Select the shader, check Absolute position in Layout, set W and H to Fill and X and Y to 0, then order it behind the content frame in the layers list.

Deciding a slider is broken because moving it changes nothing.

Check its prerequisite in the effect’s reference: Lens Distortion’s color controls need Spread above 0, Waves’ frequency needs amplitude above 0, and Paper Texture’s fold sizes need Folds above 0.

Upgrading @paper-design/shaders and shipping a preset that now looks different.

Pin the version from the copied header, read the changelog and migration guide (Paper Texture changed in 0.0.81), and re-approve the still before release.

Paper's canvas is real HTML and CSS, and its MCP server lets AI agents read and change it. These chapters cover connecting agents, running several at once, reusing patterns, shipping to code and publishing.

Chapter 10Part 4 · Agents and code

MCP: connect the agent to a specific design context

MCP makes Paper accessible to an agent. Reliable work comes from giving that connection an exact file, a bounded change and an observable result.

The connection is the beginning of the workflow

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the connection through which an agent calls Paper’s design operations. In Paper, the server runs locally inside Paper Desktop: opening the app starts it, and it reads and writes the files open there, including files in background tabs. Paper in a browser does not provide this local server, and the desktop dashboard alone is not enough; the agent needs Paper Desktop running with a design file open. The connection does not replace design judgment or decide which file should change. An agent still needs to understand the material, locate the relevant frame and distinguish a requested edit from surrounding content that must remain stable.

As of September 2026, the quickest setup starts inside Paper: with nothing selected, the right panel’s MCP section has a Connect your agent button that adds Paper to a chosen client in one click. Paper’s documentation names the Paper CLI as the current route for most clients: the client launches it with the argument mcp, and it relays to the desktop app. Spring 2026 tutorials register a local HTTP address instead, http://127.0.0.1:29979/mcp, which Paper Desktop still serves while a file is open. Use one route per client rather than mixing configuration fragments from different versions, and restart the agent session after any change, since a running session does not load new tools. A successful connection establishes access; it does not establish that the agent has identified the correct design context.

Connection grants access; an exact target and a reviewable change make the work reliable.

The principle of chapter 10

Study 10 · change it yourself
Interactive study: MCP. It runs in the web edition with JavaScript.

Read before writing

A useful first request asks the agent to identify the target file and describe the selected frame’s structure without editing it. One of Paper’s tutorials opens with a question as plain as “Are we connected to the Paper MCP?”, and the agent answers with the open file, page, artboard and its size, node count and fonts, read through tools such as get_basic_info and get_selection. That small read establishes shared context. If the description refers to a different page or misses the intended component, correct the target before requesting a redesign.

Since August 2026, Paper Desktop opens files as tabs, and agents can work in any open file, including tabs in the background. That makes explicit targeting more important. Name the file (“In the Learn Section file in Paper, …”) or paste its link from Copy link (⌘L); select a frame before pressing ⌘L to link that frame instead. “The active Paper file” means the tab in front when the agent starts, so stay on it until the agent is working. A good task names the file, page or frame and the outcome in one sentence: “In the comparison frame of this file, align the existing values without changing the labels.” That sentence is a briefing pattern, not a special command syntax.

Comments make a target even more precise. Press C, click a layer and write the request; the comment stays pinned to that layer, so a short prompt such as “I left comments on this frame. Check it out and implement those changes.” gives the agent both the list and the locations. The agent can list and read comment threads and mark them resolved, but it cannot write comments; that part stays with you.

After reading, the agent can make a bounded structural or style change. Good write scope describes the smallest coherent unit that owns the problem: adjusting a row’s layout is clearer than requesting a whole-screen redesign to repair one column. For bigger transformations, Paper’s tutorials duplicate the frame first and have the agent change the copy. When the agent brings in content or values from elsewhere, such as a document, a Slack canvas or the codebase’s CSS variables, name the source and say whether the values are real or placeholders.

Make the result inspectable

Ask for the resulting frame to be inspected after the change. A tool response reports that an operation happened; the rendered frame shows whether it produced the intended design. In Paper’s Claude Code tutorial, the agent finishes by taking a screenshot of its artboard and running a review checkpoint on spacing, typography, contrast, alignment, clipping and repetition before it summarizes. Ask for the same, plus an account of anything missing or unresolved, rather than treating successful execution as proof of visual quality.

Paper shows where an agent is working: animated dots replace the file icon on its tab, a dotted pattern runs above the artboard it is editing, and its avatar joins the presence row at the top of the right panel. The agent removes the artboard marker when it finishes (the finish_working_on_nodes tool). Check the frame yourself, then close the loop: have the agent resolve the comment threads it fully addressed and leave the rest open with a reason.

The agent does not track edits you make by hand. Paper’s advice is to have it re-read the canvas before the next request. A useful handoff names the target, the changed properties and the evidence used to judge them, which gives the next collaborator, or the next session, a clear starting point. The loop also works away from the desk: with Remote Control in Claude Code, the screenshots the agent sends back are how you review from a phone.

In Paper

How it works in Paper

As of September 2026, Paper’s MCP server runs locally inside Paper Desktop and works on the files open there, including background tabs. You connect a client with the one-click Connect your agent dialog, the Paper CLI, or the older local HTTP address. Its tools (36 in an installed client, October 2026) read files, pages, selections, structure, styles, tokens and comments, write HTML and styles, export, and capture screenshots. Comments pinned to layers become instructions, and Remote Control in Claude Code lets you steer a desktop session from a phone.

Checked against the videos and documentation as of September 2026. Paper ships often; the release timeline in the reference shows what changed when.

Connect an agent from inside Paper

  1. Open Paper Desktop on a design file. With nothing selected, click Connect your agent in the right panel’s MCP section.
  2. In the dialog’s left column, choose your client: Cursor, Claude, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, VS Code, OpenCode, Codex, Codex CLI, Antigravity or Other agents.
  3. Step 1, Install Paper Desktop, is already checked. In step 2, click the client’s button, for example Add to GitHub Copilot (“Add Paper to GitHub Copilot as an MCP server”) or Add to Cursor (“Add through the Cursor Marketplace”).
  4. A toast confirms it (“Added to GitHub Copilot”) and tells you to restart the client. Restart it.
  5. Check that Paper is switched on in the client. In GitHub Copilot, open Customize › MCP and turn on Paper under Installed.
  6. Test with one of the dialog’s prompts: “Create a basic Hello World frame in Paper”, “Create 3 color tokens and make a swatch in Paper” or “Generate an image of a beautiful sunset in Paper”.
  7. For a manual setup, expand Or, install manually. Paper’s docs describe the generic setup as a stdio server whose command is the Paper CLI path from Paper Desktop, with the single argument mcp.
Shown at 0:56

Connect Claude Code from the terminal

  1. Install Claude Code if needed (the video uses curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash), run claude and accept the folder trust check.
  2. Add Paper. Paper’s docs (early October 2026) use the plugin: claude plugin marketplace add paper-design/agent-plugins, then claude plugin install paper-desktop@paper.
  3. The May 2026 video registers the HTTP server instead, claude mcp add paper --transport http http://127.0.0.1:29979/mcp --scope user, which Claude Code saves to the user config in ~/.claude.json.
  4. Restart Claude Code. A server added inside a running session does not load its tools; Claude says so and suggests checking with claude mcp list.
  5. Open Paper Desktop on a design file (not Paper in a browser, and not only the dashboard), then run /mcp and look for paper marked connected.
  6. Start prompts with “In Paper” so the agent builds on the canvas, for example “In Paper, design a basic social media home page”.
Shown at 1:05

Install the Paper plugin in Cursor

  1. Open Cursor Settings (⇧⌘J), go to the plugin marketplace, search for Paper and click Get.
  2. Or paste /add-plugin paper-desktop into a New Agent chat and pick Paper in the Add Plugin popover.
  3. On the card (Paper · Verified by Cursor), choose Add for Myself or Add to Project, then click Add Plugin.
  4. Check that the paper server is listed in Cursor Settings › Tools & MCP. If the agent cannot see it, reload the Cursor window or toggle the server off and on.
  5. Keep Paper Desktop running with a design file open whenever the agent works.
⌘⇧J
Shown at 0:24

Point each agent at the right file, page and frame

  1. Open every file the agents need as a tab; the + at the end of the tab bar opens a new or existing file.
  2. Start each prompt with its file: “In the Learn Section file in Paper, create 5 variations …”.
  3. Or paste the file’s link instead of its name: click Copy link (⌘L) at the top of the right panel and paste it into the prompt. Given a link, the agent loads the Paper guide and opens that file (open_file) before anything else.
  4. To point at one frame, select it, press ⌘L and paste the link, or say “the selected frame”, since the agent can read your selection.
  5. Write “in the active Paper file” only if you stay on that tab until the agent has started; after that it keeps its file and you can switch tabs.
  6. Name the page when the work spans pages. In the demo, one agent read the token frames on a Tokens page and applied them to a frame on the Design page.
  7. Watch the tab bar: a tab with an agent working in it shows animated dots instead of its file icon, even in the background.
⌘L
Shown at 0:42

Run a read, change, verify pass from comments

  1. Press C (or click the comment button in the left toolbar), click the exact layer to change, type the request in Leave a comment and click Send. Keep one request per comment.
  2. Tell the agent where the comments are, with the frame’s link if several files are open: “I left comments on this frame. Check it out and implement those changes.”
  3. Ask it to read first: list the open threads on that frame (list_comment_threads, get_comment_thread) and describe the frame’s structure before editing.
  4. Have it change only the commented layers, editing the existing nodes rather than rebuilding the frame.
  5. Ask for a screenshot of the changed frame and one line per thread: what changed, or why it could not be done.
  6. Have it resolve only the threads it fully addressed (set_comment_thread_status), then open the comments list in the right panel and use the resolved toggle to see what is still open.
C
Shown at 0:08

Continue a Claude Code session from your phone

  1. On the computer, open Paper Desktop on the file and start Claude Code in a terminal. In July 2026, Remote Control had to start from the terminal, not from the Claude desktop app.
  2. Inside the session, type /remote-control or /rc. Your phone shows a notification that the session is ready to control.
  3. Keep the computer awake: in System Settings › Lock Screen, set Turn display off on battery when inactive and Turn display off on power adapter when inactive to For 3 hours, as in the video.
  4. In the Claude mobile app, open the Code tab and tap the session marked Connected under Sessions; the whole conversation is there.
  5. Type or dictate prompts that name the frame, the source of any content and where the result goes, such as a duplicated frame.
  6. Review the screenshots the agent sends back in the chat; tap one to see it full screen.

Limits and what is coming

  • As of September 2026, the MCP server runs only inside Paper Desktop with the target file open. Paper in a browser has no local server (its WebMCP support, added in September 2026, is for in-browser agents on partner sites). Remote MCP, for cloud agents without the desktop app, was announced as coming next on 28 September 2026.
  • The tool set (36 tools in an installed client, October 2026) can list and read comment threads and set them to resolved or open, but it cannot create comments, delete pages or files, or add shaders.
  • Remote Control, as shown in July 2026, starts only from a Claude Code session in a terminal and needs the computer awake with Paper open for the whole session. There is no Paper mobile app.
  • Paper’s pricing page in early October 2026 lists 100 MCP tool calls per week on the Free plan and 1 million on Pro. Image generation through the MCP also draws on your image allowance.

Build it in Paper

  1. Open Paper Desktop on the file you want to change. With nothing selected, click Connect your agent in the right panel’s MCP section, pick your client, click the button in step 2 (for example Add to Cursor), restart the client and confirm that Paper is listed (/mcp in Claude Code).
  2. Select the target frame, press ⌘L and paste the link into a first prompt: “In Paper, describe the structure of this frame without changing anything.” If the answer names another file or page, correct the target.
  3. Press C and pin one comment on each layer that needs work, then ask for one bounded change: “Implement the open comments on this frame by editing the existing layers, and keep every label unchanged.”
  4. Ask the agent to screenshot the frame, review spacing, typography, contrast, alignment and clipping, and list what it changed and what it could not do.
  5. Check the result yourself, have the agent resolve only the threads it fully addressed, and after any hand edit tell it to re-read the canvas before the next request.

Check before you move on

  • Did the agent’s first answer name the file, page and frame you meant, before it changed anything?
  • Did the change stay inside the layers you named or commented on, with every label and value you asked to keep unchanged?
  • Has the agent shown a screenshot of the changed frame and said what it changed and what it could not do?
  • Are the threads it addressed resolved, and is every other thread still open?
  • If you edited the frame by hand, did the agent re-read it before its next change?

Common mistakes

Adding the Paper server inside a running agent session and prompting straight away; the tools are not loaded yet.

Restart the client after any setup change, then confirm Paper is listed: /mcp in Claude Code, Cursor Settings › Tools & MCP, or Customize › MCP in GitHub Copilot.

Opening the design in a browser, or leaving only the desktop dashboard open, and expecting the agent to reach it.

Keep Paper Desktop running with the target file open in a tab for the whole session.

Writing “this file” or “the active Paper file” and then switching tabs before the agent starts, so it works in whichever tab is in front.

Name the file or paste its link (⌘L) in the prompt. If you rely on the active file, stay on that tab until its dots appear.

Reworking a frame by hand and then asking for the next change; the agent still works from what it read before.

Begin the next prompt by asking the agent to re-read the canvas, or that frame, before it edits.

Chapter 11Part 4 · Agents and code

Parallel AI agents: keep one coherent design

Parallel work is useful when its parts are independent. A shared canvas needs clear ownership, a common reference and a deliberate moment of integration.

Parallelize alternatives, not uncertainty

Several agents can produce more material quickly, but more material is not automatically a better design. Give them different questions to answer. One can explore a denser hierarchy, another a clearer comparison and another a more explicit empty state. Each direction should preserve the same required content so the final comparison evaluates design choices rather than accidental omissions.

The Paper and Conductor demonstration shows the bounded version. The brief names its references (a captured hero, a changelog and a roadmap page), fixes the count at three iterations and ties one of them to the changelog. The agent returns three labeled directions on separate artboards, and the presenters choose among them before any code is written. Sending three agents the same vague instruction merely multiplies the ambiguous outcomes you must inspect.

Parallel does not always mean several agents. One agent can spread a brief across many artboards: asked for as many good meditation home screens as possible in five minutes, Opus 5.5 named six mood directions, created six artboards and built them breadth-first, headers on all six before any hero, so every variant reached the same stage at the same time.

Independent ownership creates useful parallelism; explicit review turns the alternatives into one coherent result.

The principle of chapter 11

Study 11 · change it yourself
Interactive study: Parallel agents. It runs in the web edition with JavaScript.

Assign ownership at the level of possible conflict

Give each design agent a named destination file, page or artboard. Separate artboards help keep alternative layouts independent, but they do not isolate every resource. A token edited in a file changes every layer bound to it in that file. A renamed frame or an edited reference can alter the context another agent is reading. The ownership rule must therefore cover shared inputs as well as visible output regions.

Paper shows where agents work: a robot avatar joins the presence row, and animated dots mark the file's tab and the artboard being edited. It does not reserve anything. In the Conductor session a second agent restyled the frames while the first was still writing them. It worked there, with a prompt that named the frames and the exact change, but steering the first agent would have been simpler. A practical arrangement is one owner for shared tokens and one agent per artboard or file, with the others proposing token changes rather than applying them.

Code work needs its own isolation. In Conductor, each new workspace is an isolated copy of the repository on its own branch, so coding agents do not collide, while a new tab inside a workspace shares that copy. Neither separates Paper: every agent writes to the same open files through Paper Desktop. When several files are open as tabs, name the file in every prompt or paste its link, so that parallel means independent work rather than simultaneous writes to the same material.

Integrate through a design decision

Compare alternatives against the same question and the same required actions. A layout can be visually attractive while dropping a necessary control: in one Paper demonstration a variant lost its add button although the agent's own checkpoint review passed it. Review the complete flow and identify the particular traits worth retaining: one hierarchy, one navigation treatment, one useful explanation. Ask for a composed revision with those named traits instead of the ambiguous instruction to combine everything good.

That review is the point where parallel work becomes one design. Keep the alternatives on the canvas long enough to explain the decision, then mark the accepted frame by name. An implementation agent should receive that exact name, not choose among unresolved drafts. In the Conductor session the presenters pasted the title “Conductor Roadmap — 02 Network Map” into the prompt; the agent read the frame with get_screenshot and get_jsx and compared a headless screenshot of its page with the Paper frame. Later feedback stays located: comments on the canvas in Paper, or comments on diff lines in the code tool.

In Paper

How it works in Paper

As of September 2026, several agents can work in Paper at once: on separate artboards of one file, or across files open as desktop tabs (since August 2026), including tabs in the background. Each agent appears as an avatar in the presence row and as animated dots on its tab and above the artboard it is editing. Paper does not lock nodes or isolate code: prompts set each agent's destination, and the harness, such as Conductor's workspaces, isolates the repository. File links, exact frame names and comments coordinate the work.

Checked against the videos and documentation as of September 2026. Paper ships often; the release timeline in the reference shows what changed when.

Explore directions on separate artboards

  1. With the file open in Paper Desktop, ask “Are we connected to the Paper MCP?”. The agent should report the file, page, artboard and size, node count and fonts.
  2. Name the frame and the count: “In Paper, design two iterations of the Social Home frame. Explore different colors and layouts.”
  3. Expect the agent to read the frame's structure and name its directions (here “Ink” and “Slate”) before it writes.
  4. Each direction appears as a new artboard beside the untouched original, named after it, such as “Social Home — Ink (Dark)”, with working dots above it while the agent builds.
  5. Check every variant against the original's controls yourself; the agent's review passed a variant that had lost its add button.
  6. Combine by naming traits and their sources: navigation from Ink, palette and side bar from Slate, a dark purple accent. The agent should state a plan with hex values before it builds.
Shown at 1:08

Give each agent its own file

  1. Open every file the agents will use as a tab in Paper Desktop. Agents can work in background tabs, so the tab in front does not matter once they have started.
  2. Start each prompt with its file: “In the Learn Section file in Paper, …”, or paste a link copied with Copy link (⌘L).
  3. Write “in the active Paper file” only if that tab stays in front until the agent has started; the agent settles on its file at the start.
  4. To give an agent a fresh file, ask it to create and name one through the MCP, for example “a new file called Musical Conductor Roadmap”. It opens as a new tab.
  5. Rename auto-named files before prompting: double-click the tab, or right-click it and choose Rename.
⌘L
Shown at 1:04

Isolate code work in Conductor

  1. Press ⌘N for a new workspace. Each workspace is an isolated copy of the repository on its own branch, so coding agents in different workspaces do not collide.
  2. Open a new tab inside a workspace instead when the job only changes Paper; tabs share the workspace's copy of the code.
  3. Set model and effort per job in the composer. The session used Opus 5 at High for the first designs and Medium for the restyle and the code port.
  4. To correct a running agent, type and press Enter to steer it; press ⌘Enter to queue the message until its turn ends.
  5. Press ⌃O to expand all tool calls, then click a call such as write_html to see its target node, mode and HTML.
⌘NEnter⌘Enter⌃O

Correct brand drift while agents run

  1. Select a heading on each agent's artboard and read Right panel › Text. The first roadmap heading read Matter, Medium, 52, not the brand's Geist.
  2. Fix a single instance by hand: click the font family field, type “gei” in the Fonts popover's search and choose Geist.
  3. For every frame, steer the agent that owns them, or give one agent a precise edit: use the Paper MCP to edit the roadmap frames, change the font from Matter to Geist and change them from light mode to dark mode.
  4. If a second agent edits frames another agent is still building, it can only follow behind; check the frames again when both have finished.
  5. Confirm each frame in the Text section and in Selection colors before anyone ports the design.
Shown at 7:08

Compare two models fairly

  1. Open two agent sessions against the same blank Paper file, one model each, at the same effort (High in the test).
  2. Paste the same prompt into both and change only the requested artboard title, such as “Fable 5 Version” and “Opus 4.8 Version”.
  3. Send both as close together as you can and note the gap; the presenter allowed about five seconds for the later start.
  4. Watch both artboards build side by side and record which run finishes first.
  5. Judge each screen against the brief, including invented content such as a $42.50 coffee, then read both summaries.
  6. Treat one screen as one sample: repeat with several screens or tasks before you settle on a model.
Shown at 0:40

Hand the accepted frame to an implementation agent

  1. Double-click the accepted artboard's title on the canvas and copy its exact name, such as “Conductor Roadmap — 02 Network Map”.
  2. In a fresh code workspace, prompt: “Look at the <name> frame in Paper and recreate that and run it locally.”
  3. Expect reads before writes: get_guide, list_files, get_basic_info, get_screenshot and get_jsx.
  4. Review the diff and the running page. In an empty repository the agent wrote a standalone index.html, served it on port 4321 and checked a headless screenshot against the Paper frame.
  5. Leave feedback where it belongs. In Conductor, select diff lines, click + in the gutter, type the note and choose Comment; it lands in the composer for the agent. In Paper, press C, click the frame, type in “Leave a comment”, choose Send, then tell the agent to read your comments.

Limits and what is coming

  • As of September 2026 the Paper MCP has no tool to reserve or lock nodes. The working dots show where an agent is busy, but two agents can edit the same frames, so ownership lives in your prompts.
  • Agents can list, read and resolve comment threads through the MCP but cannot create comments (tool list as of October 2026); people write the comments.
  • Remote MCP, for cloud agents with no Paper Desktop open, and per-file permissions were announced as coming next on 28 September 2026, not shipped.
  • MCP tool calls count against a weekly plan allowance: 100 on Free and 1M on Pro (pricing as of October 2026). Several agents running at once use it up faster.
