Build it in Paper

  1. Gather the shared references on one page of a Paper file and name each frame. Capture live pages with Paper Snapshot (⌘Enter takes the whole page) and paste them with ⌘V.
  2. Give each agent one question and one destination: a named artboard for an alternative in the same file, or its own file open as a tab. Start each prompt with the file name or a link from Copy link (⌘L), then the fonts, the theme and the content every version must keep.
  3. Run the agents and follow the working dots on tabs and artboards. Correct drift in the agent that owns the frames (in Conductor, Enter steers a running agent and ⌘Enter queues a message) instead of sending a second agent onto the same frames.
  4. Review every alternative against one checklist: required actions present, the brand font in the Text section, only brand values in Selection colors. Fix one-off issues by hand, for example a font through the Fonts popover's search.
  5. Name the accepted frame, paste its exact title into a fresh code workspace's prompt, and have the agent compare its build with a screenshot of that frame before you review the diff.

Check before you move on

  • Does every agent's prompt name its file and destination artboard, or carry a Copy link?
  • Do all alternatives keep the source frame's required content and actions, counted one by one?
  • Are the brand fonts and theme stated in every brief, and do the Text section and Selection colors confirm them on each frame?
  • Did compared runs share the prompt, effort, file and start time, with only one thing changed?
  • Is exactly one frame marked as accepted, and does the implementation prompt quote its exact name?

Common mistakes

Sending several agents the same vague prompt and letting them choose where to write.

Give each agent one question and one named artboard or file, state how many directions you want and list what must stay fixed.

Leaving the typeface and theme to the agent. In the Conductor session it set headings in Matter, Paper's font, on light frames, for a team that wanted Geist and dark mode.

Name fonts, theme and palette in the brief. If drift appears, steer the agent that owns the frames or give one agent an explicit from-and-to edit, then recheck the Text section.

Trusting an agent's self-review. The Slate variant passed its checkpoint review without its add button.

Check each variant against a list of the original's controls before you combine or accept anything.

Assuming separate Conductor workspaces keep agents apart in Paper.

Workspaces isolate code only. Separate Paper work by artboard or file and name it in each prompt; use a tab rather than a workspace for canvas-only edits.

Chapter 12Part 4 · Agents and code

Repeat the rule, then vary the content

A reusable pattern preserves a relationship across different content and states. Visual similarity alone does not establish that relationship.

Find the repeated decision

Two cards can share a border radius while behaving quite differently. That is a shared style, not necessarily a shared component. A reusable pattern begins with a repeated responsibility: a track row relates a title to its artist, length and play state; a metric row relates a label to several values; a notice connects a condition to an action. The responsibility explains which parts should stay stable.

Describe the pattern through its inputs and states. A row might accept a name, a secondary label, a value and a selection state. A missing value is then a defined state rather than a reason to redraw the row. A long name is ordinary input, not an exceptional design. This way of thinking lets the layout accommodate variation without losing its visual identity.

Write that contract where the pattern lives. In Paper’s September 2026 components tutorial, the agent that rebuilt a music app’s components set a one-line spec beside each one without being asked. The cover card states its art radius, its title and byline sizes and its two widths, 148 on a shelf and 112 in a grid. The track row fixes its lanes (number 20, art 34, a title that fills, album 120, time 40, save 24, more 24) at a height of 52, and a playing row gains an amber dot while nothing else changes. Ask for that line whenever you build a pattern.

A useful pattern repeats a responsibility while making legitimate variation explicit.

The principle of chapter 12

Study 12 · change it yourself
Interactive study: Reuse. It runs in the web edition with JavaScript.

Ground the pattern in an existing product

The repository-to-canvas tutorial brings a music app’s existing components and tokens into Paper, explores a new section with real content and returns the chosen result to the codebase. The valuable starting point is the existing product vocabulary. Reusing it preserves familiar behavior: when the new section reached the code, its cards already opened their playlist pages, because they were the app’s own card component.

Be exact about what Paper links today. As of September 2026 the canvas has no native components: Paper announced components on the canvas as coming soon on 28 September, and its public roadmap lists components with slots as coming soon and the use of code components on the canvas as in progress. A duplicate made with ⌘D or ⌥-drag is an independent copy. What stays linked is tokens: change a token in the Theme tab and every layer bound to it in the file updates. A component rebuilt by an agent, or captured with Paper Snapshot, is a set of editable frames, not an instance.

You can still define a reliable pattern today with a canonical frame, named tokens, documented inputs and repeated specimens. Keep the canonical specimen next to demanding variants: the ordinary state, the selected state, long text and unavailable information. These variants are more useful than many nearly identical copies because they reveal the pattern’s limits. If one case needs a different structure, decide whether it is a legitimate variant or a different responsibility that deserves its own component.

Preserve meaning when you repeat

Consistency should make exceptions easier to see. A selected row must remain related to its siblings while being clearly selected. An unavailable value should preserve the comparison lane while explaining its absence. When every state adds another badge, color or panel, the pattern can become harder to read despite being technically comprehensive.

Vary one rule at a time, on a copy. In the tutorial, the agent duplicated the finished section, named the copy after its single change (For you section · Grid 112), swapped the 148-pixel covers for 112-pixel ones and reported the cost: nine covers now fit in the row, but longer bylines clip at that size. The original stayed untouched, so the comparison was fair, and the designer kept the larger cards.

Reuse the important rule, not every dimension or sentence. On the code side, the same contract becomes a component’s properties and states; on the canvas, it keeps the design explanation stable until Paper’s native components arrive. Say clearly which relationships the tool enforces (token bindings) and which the workflow maintains (copies, specimens and agent updates).

In Paper

How it works in Paper

As of September 2026 Paper has no native components. Duplicates (⌘D, ⌥-drag or Duplicate in the right-click menu) are independent copies with no link back. What stays linked is tokens: change one in the Theme tab and every bound layer in the file updates, as with a CSS custom property. For a code-based system, an agent can rebuild repository components as editable, token-bound layers, and Paper Snapshot can copy them from a live site. Native components with slots were announced as coming soon.

Checked against the videos and documentation as of September 2026. Paper ships often; the release timeline in the reference shows what changed when.

Rebuild code components on the canvas with an agent

  1. Open a new Paper file and make sure your agent is connected; with nothing selected, the right panel’s MCP section has a Connect your agent button for the setup.
  2. In an agent session inside your repository, name the flow you are about to design and the components it will need (the demo listed cover cards, artist cards and track cards), and ask the agent to build them in the open Paper file before any design work.
  3. Watch the canvas: the agent’s avatar joins yours at the top of the right panel, and a dotted pattern above a frame marks the one it is reading or writing.
  4. Review the sheet. The demo’s, For You · Components, had numbered sections (01 Cover card, 02 Person, 03 Track row, 04 Section header), a dark and a light version of each, semantic layer names such as Cover · Bloom and a one-line spec per section.
  5. Select a text layer and read the right panel: Fill showed the token text, the font family sans, and size and line height showed 14 and 20 as token chips, because the agent had imported and bound the codebase’s tokens on its own.
Shown at 0:28

Copy a live component or page with Paper Snapshot, then fit it into a layout

  1. Install the Paper Snapshot extension in Chrome and open the live page. The first time on a site, Chrome’s Extensions menu lists Paper Snapshot under Access requested; click it to grant access.
  2. Turn Snapshot on, hover the element and click to copy it. Press ⌘Return instead to copy the whole page.
  3. Paste in Paper. The layers are editable and match the coded component, but they are named Frame, keep raw CSS under Other styles (margins, max-width, font-synthesis) and have no token bindings.
  4. To place a section inside a captured page, copy the section, select the page’s content column and paste. The frame arrives with Absolute position ticked and floats over the layout.
  5. Untick Absolute position (right panel, under Flex) so the section joins the column’s flex flow, then drag it to its place in the order.
⌘Return
Shown at 3:15

Try a variant on a duplicate

  1. Decide on the single change you want to test and keep the current section as the original.
  2. Ask the agent to duplicate the section frame and apply that change to the copy (the demo asked to see the section with the smaller card components instead of the larger ones).
  3. The agent leaves the original untouched, places the copy beside it and names it after the change: For you section · Grid 112.
  4. Read its report of the tradeoff: 112-pixel covers instead of 148, nine fit in the row, bylines shortened to curator names, and longer lines clip at that size.
  5. Compare the two side by side and keep the better one; the demo kept the larger cards.
Shown at 3:56

Send the chosen frame back to code

  1. Give the winning frame a name nobody can mistake: the demo double-clicks the frame’s name on the canvas and types FINAL.
  2. In the agent, point to that frame and to the destination, for example by asking it to take the For You section from the final frame in Paper and add it to the Explore page of the codebase.
  3. The agent reads the frame and edits existing files rather than creating parallel ones; the demo reported four files, among them the Explore page component and its stylesheet, and checked the page with browser actions before reporting.
  4. Open the page locally and use it. The coded section matched the frame, and clicking a card opened its playlist page, because the cards were the app’s existing component.
Shown at 4:55

Duplicate specimens with a repeated offset

  1. Select the canonical layer or frame.
  2. Hold ⌥ and drag to place a copy; set a rotation on the copy if the pattern needs one (the demo typed 30°).
  3. Press ⌘D: each new duplicate repeats the same offset and rotation (since August 2026), which in the demo turned one bar into a ring of bars.
  4. Change each copy’s content for the state it represents and rename it after that state.
  5. Remember that the copies are independent: a later fix to the original has to be repeated on each copy, by hand or by an agent.
⌥Drag⌘D
Shown at 4:42

Change a shared value once with a token

  1. Switch the left panel from Design to Theme. It lists the file’s tokens by type, with a count, a search field and + to create one.
  2. Click a token to edit its Name and Value. For a color, pick a new value or point it at another token; the picker shows Previous and New side by side.
  3. Every layer bound to that token updates at once across the file. Close the picker to keep the new value.
  4. To turn a raw fill into a token, select the layer, click the token icon beside the Fill value, press + at the top of the token list, then name and save the new token.
  5. Check bindings in Selection colors at the bottom of the right panel: bound colors appear by token name, with the number of layers that use them.

Copy styles / Paste stylesRight-click menu (⌥⌘C / ⌥⌘V)Transfers one layer’s styling to another in a single step; the result is a one-time copy, not a link.Listed in the menu; not demonstrated in the videos.

Limits and what is coming

  • As of 28 September 2026 Paper had no native components: components on the canvas were announced as coming soon, and the public roadmap listed components with slots as coming soon and code components on the canvas as in progress. Until they ship, a fix to an original must be repeated on every copy.
  • A component an agent rebuilds from code is a design representation, not a linked instance: when the code changes, the canvas copy changes only if you ask the agent to rebuild it.
  • Tokens link layers within one file; tokens copied to another file form an independent set that needs explicit updates (Paper’s token documentation, September 2026).
  • Snapshot captures carry no token bindings and use generic Frame names, and Figma components pasted into Paper arrive detached.

Build it in Paper

  1. With your agent connected (right panel › MCP › Connect your agent), ask it to rebuild one repeated unit from your codebase on its own sheet, bound to the codebase’s tokens, with a one-line spec per component: sizes, radius, type and states.
  2. Select a text layer in the rebuilt unit and check that Fill and Text show token chips rather than raw values; turn any raw fill into a token from the token icon beside it (+ at the top of the token list).
  3. Place specimens beside the canonical frame with ⌥-drag and ⌘D: ordinary, selected, long-content and unavailable-data states, each renamed after its state.
  4. Try a variant on a duplicated section named after its one change, and keep the untouched original next to it for comparison.
  5. Rename the chosen frame (double-click its name on the canvas), ask the agent to build it into the existing page with the same code components, and click through the result in the browser.

Check before you move on

  • Can you state in one line the responsibility this pattern repeats, and the inputs and states it accepts?
  • Does every shared value in the canonical frame show a token chip rather than a raw value?
  • Are the ordinary, selected, long-content and unavailable-data specimens on the canvas beside the canonical frame?
  • If you changed the original now, do you know which copies would need the same change?
  • Does the frame you will send to code use the codebase’s own components, so their behavior comes with them?

Common mistakes

Treating duplicates as instances: fixing the original and assuming its copies follow.

As of September 2026, copies are independent. Put shared values in tokens so they propagate, and when the structure changes, ask the agent to apply the change to every copy, then check each one.

Exploring a variant by editing the approved section itself.

Duplicate the section first (⌘D, or ask the agent), name the copy after its single change and compare it with the untouched original.

Reusing a Snapshot capture as it was pasted.

Have an agent rename the generic Frame layers and bind colors and type to your tokens, and review the raw CSS under Other styles, before anyone builds on it.

A pasted section floats over the layout instead of joining it.

Untick Absolute position in the right panel so the frame rejoins its parent’s flex flow, then drag it into place.

Chapter 13Part 4 · Agents and code

Carry the design’s intent into working code

The handoff is complete when the implemented product preserves the accepted relationships, content and behavior at the sizes people use.

A frame specifies appearance and relationships

A canvas can describe where content sits, how it is grouped and which visual states matter. It cannot answer every behavior question through appearance alone. A search field needs matching rules, an empty result needs wording, and a scrolled header needs a defined response. The implementation brief should make those decisions explicit so the developer or agent does not have to invent them from a still image.

Paper’s push-to-code tutorial shows how quickly those questions surface. The redesign showed one category selected, so before writing code the agent asked three questions, starting with what the All item should show (every category stacked under its heading, or one flat grid) and whether choosing a category should change the URL. Draw the states you care about as their own artboards, as the presenter did with a scrolled state, and answer the rest when the agent asks.

Start from the accepted frame, not an old screenshot of an earlier draft. Ask the agent to read its structure, styles, token references and assets through Paper’s MCP, and treat the screenshot only as a visual check. Pixels mislead: in Paper’s email tutorial, an agent judging a manual edit from a screenshot called the new footer color #455574, then read the computed styles and reported the actual #415377.

Exact design extraction provides the starting point; the running task establishes completion.

The principle of chapter 13

Study 13 · change it yourself
Interactive study: Code. It runs in the web edition with JavaScript.

Reuse the product’s working behavior

The Learn-page tutorial gives the agent a redesign and a scrolled state, names the existing components to reuse, and then tests the running result. This is a stronger handoff than requesting a visual clone of one screen. It acknowledges that the design is entering a product with established navigation, data and interaction rules: the agent copied the app’s existing sticky-header pattern and used its existing search field, so search worked with no new logic.

The exported or generated representation still needs an application context. A visual button must connect to the intended action. A selected row must have a meaningful state. A chart must receive validated values rather than the convenient sample shown on the canvas. Motion is handled the same way: Paper’s own website was designed statically in Paper, shaders included, and its animations were prompted on top of the file while an agent built the Next.js site.

For a manual handoff, Paper copies a selection as Tailwind (⌥T), as React with inline styles (Copy as React CSS, ⌥R) or as a PNG (⇧⌘C), from the right-click Copy as… menu and, since September 2026, from a copy icon in the Export section. Select a coherent nested unit, ideally one that is already a code component, rather than a whole page. Treat this as a present capability with its own scope: native Tailwind integration was still listed as in progress on Paper’s roadmap.

Compare the result at the level of the task

The first visual comparison should use the same viewport, content and state as the accepted frame. Differences then have a clear meaning. If the fonts, data and width all change together, it becomes difficult to identify whether a mismatch comes from implementation or from a different test condition. Resolve the controlled comparison before evaluating broader variation.

Then use the feature. Search for something absent, move through the navigation, resize the page and inspect the last item. The tutorial’s review of categories, scrolling and search illustrates this shift from appearance to behavior. An observed problem can belong to the frame, the extraction, the implementation or the review, so trace it to its stage before patching the code.

Review the change itself as carefully as the page. Read the agent’s summary of files changed and patterns reused, then the diff. In Paper’s token round trip, the agent changed only the five colors in the selection and listed two other variables that still used the old hue instead of silently changing them; that report is a decision handed back to you.

In Paper

How it works in Paper

Paper’s canvas is HTML and CSS, so there is no translation layer between a frame and code. As of September 2026 there are two routes out. An agent connected over the MCP reads the frame (get_jsx returns JSX with Tailwind classes or inline styles, get_computed_styles returns exact CSS) and edits your codebase. Or you copy a selection as Tailwind, React with inline styles or PNG from the right-click menu or the Export section. Behavior and motion are specified in prompts and built in code.

Checked against the videos and documentation as of September 2026. Paper ships often; the release timeline in the reference shows what changed when.

Connect an agent to Paper

  1. Open Paper Desktop and the file you will work on; the MCP server runs inside the desktop app.
  2. With nothing selected, click Connect your agent in the right panel’s MCP section.
  3. Pick your harness (Cursor, Claude, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, VS Code, OpenCode, Codex, Codex CLI, Antigravity or Other agents) and click its Add to … button, or expand Or, install manually.
  4. Restart the agent if needed and switch Paper on in its MCP list (the demo did both for GitHub Copilot), then run one of the dialog’s test prompts, such as creating a Hello World frame in Paper.
  5. Approve tool calls as they come. In Claude Code, the second option, Yes, and don’t ask again, stops the prompts for that Paper tool in the current folder; the March 2026 tutorial recommends it for read tools and write tools alike.
  6. Older route, still supported: the March 2026 tutorial ran claude mcp add --scope user --transport http paper http://127.0.0.1:29979/mcp in a normal terminal (not inside Claude) and confirmed the connection with /mcp.
Shown at 0:56

Lay out code values on the canvas

  1. In an agent session inside your repository, ask it to read a style file and arrange its values on the open Paper canvas (the demo used the repository’s colors.css).
  2. Approve the tool calls: the agent calls get_basic_info, reads the file, checks typefaces with get_font_family_info and writes the board with write_html, which produces real HTML and CSS layers.
  3. Check the board. The demo’s Color System board listed 22 tokens in three groups (Chromatic, Neutrals, Surfaces); each swatch showed a display name, its CSS variable, its oklch value and the usage note taken from the code comment.
  4. Let the agent review its own screenshot. Here it found clipped bottom padding and set the artboard height to 1040px with update_styles.
Shown at 1:11

Edit values on the canvas and write them back

  1. Select the swatches to change (the demo selected five: four blues and the brand color).
  2. In Selection colors, edit a row’s values, shown as lightness %, chroma, hue° / alpha; every selected layer using that color updates. The demo moved the hue from 258 to between 268 and 273.
  3. Keep the selection and ask the agent to bring the colors you modified in your Paper selection back into the CSS file.
  4. The agent reads Get Selection, Get Computed Styles and Get Node Info, maps each value to its variable and edits the file.
  5. Review the diff (Keep File or Undo File in Cursor). The demo changed exactly the five selected variables and named two others that shared the old hue without touching them.
Shown at 5:44

Build a frame into an existing codebase

  1. Name the frames clearly and draw extra states as their own artboards (the demo: Learn — Redesign and Learn — Redesign Scrolled).
  2. In your IDE, open a new agent and attach the file the design replaces (index.tsx in the demo).
  3. Prompt with four parts: build the named frame from the open Paper file; update the attached file; keep the scroll behavior drawn on the canvas, which should match scrolling elsewhere in the app; and wherever the design uses an existing code component, such as the search field, use it instead of creating a new one.
  4. Raise the effort for a real build: the demo switched Claude Opus 5 from Low to High and turned on Fast.
  5. Answer the agent’s questions (three in the demo; the first asked what the All category should show), then read its summary of files changed, patterns reused and how the behavior works.
  6. Run the page locally and exercise it before choosing Keep All.
Shown at 1:32

Copy one component as code

  1. Hold ⌘ and click to select the nested layer directly (the demo: a 216 × 32 Settings tab in the sidebar).
  2. Right-click › Copy as… › Copy as Tailwind (⌥T) or Copy as React CSS (⌥R); Copy as PNG (⇧⌘C) copies an image instead.
  3. Since September 2026 the same three options also sit behind the copy icon beside Export in the right panel.
  4. Paste into your code. React CSS output opens with a comment (from Paper, the layer’s Paper link and the date) followed by an exported function whose elements carry inline style objects.
  5. Prefer a unit that is already a code component; a whole frame copies too, but the useful difference gets buried.
⌘Click⌥T⌥R
Shown at 3:05

Read a selection the way an agent should

  1. Select the design in Paper and ask the agent to convert your selected design to code.
  2. get_selection identifies it (the demo: a 1440 × 900 PlaylistPage frame).
  3. get_screenshot captures it at scale 2 as a visual reference, and get_tree_summary lists its structure (Header, TrackList with 7 children, PlaybackBar).
  4. The agent reads the project’s own types, then get_computed_styles for exact values (Inter, a 12px gap) and get_jsx for a subtree’s markup.
  5. It writes components in the project’s conventions (components/playlist-header.tsx in the demo). Paper’s MCP instructions ask agents to take sizes and colors from these tools and to use screenshots only for checking.

Build it in Paper

  1. Name the accepted frame and draw each behavior state that matters (scrolled, empty, selected) as its own artboard beside it.
  2. Connect your agent (right panel › MCP › Connect your agent) and prompt with four parts: the frame’s name in the open Paper file, the file to update, the behavior to keep and where it already exists in the app, and an instruction to reuse existing components.
  3. Answer the agent’s questions, then read its summary of files changed and components reused before you keep the changes.
  4. For a single component, ⌘-click to reach the nested layer, then right-click › Copy as… › Copy as Tailwind (⌥T) or Copy as React CSS (⌥R).
  5. Run the page at the frame’s width with the same content and compare; then test the task: switch categories, scroll, search for something absent and narrow the window.

Check before you move on

  • Is every state the code must handle either drawn as its own artboard or written into the prompt?
  • Did the values come from get_jsx and get_computed_styles rather than from a screenshot?
  • Does the implementation reuse the components the design came from, instead of new look-alikes?
  • Have you compared the running page with the frame at the same width, content and state?
  • Have you used the feature: navigation, scrolling, a search with no result, a narrow window?

Common mistakes

Handing over a still frame and letting the agent guess the behavior.

Draw states such as scrolled or selected as separate artboards, name the existing pattern to match, and answer the agent’s questions before it writes code.

Letting the agent recreate components the app already has.

Say it in the prompt: wherever the design uses an existing code component, use that component instead of creating a new one.

Copying a whole page as Tailwind to change one element.

⌘-click the nested layer that matches a code component and copy only that, or use the agent route for page-level changes.

Keeping the agent’s changes without reading them.

Read the summary and the diff; confirm that only the intended files or variables changed, and decide on the related values the agent reports.

Chapter 14Part 4 · Agents and code

Publish an artifact that survives leaving the canvas

An export is a new rendering in a new context. Its quality depends on the frame you select, the format you choose and the result you inspect.

Choose the format for the reader’s job

An image communicates a fixed appearance. A PDF can preserve a sequence of pages and searchable text. A website can add navigation, responsive layout and interaction. These formats serve different reading tasks. Choose the deliverable according to what the reader needs to do, rather than treating every output as an interchangeable container for the same screenshot.

Paper’s outputs map onto those jobs. As of September 2026 a frame exports as PNG, JPG, AVIF, WebP or PDF at a chosen scale; a copy command puts a PNG, Tailwind or React CSS on the clipboard; video export covers moving work such as shaders on the Pro plan; and an email reaches its readers through an agent and an email service rather than as a file. Because Paper renders with HTML and CSS, its PDFs go through the browser’s print path and keep real, searchable text.

The source frame matters as much as the export format. A frame designed for a wide screen may produce tiny labels when fitted onto a page. A useful publication layout gives the reader a deliberate sequence, appropriate type size and a meaningful crop. In Paper the frame also names the file, and in a combined PDF its position on the canvas sets the page order, so exporting the right selection is the first design decision.

The delivered artifact is the result to judge, not the export button’s success message.

The principle of chapter 14

Study 14 · change it yourself
Interactive study: Export. It runs in the web edition with JavaScript.

Inspect what the exported file actually contains

Paper’s PDF tutorial selects frames and demonstrates single, separate and combined exports, then searches the exported text. That final action is part of the lesson. The presence of a PDF file does not establish that the text remains useful, the page order is correct or the content fits comfortably inside the chosen dimensions.

Read the export in the environment where it will be used. Check a page at a comfortable reading size, inspect small labels and look at images whose quality may change with resampling. Search for a distinctive word and select a sentence. If the artifact includes links, test the links rather than assuming they survived because they were visible in the design.

A still file cannot show a shader’s movement or an interface’s states by itself. Export a meaningful still, explain the behavior, and provide a working reference where it matters: a video export for motion, the coded page for interaction. Renderers change too: in September 2026 Paper began rendering images and videos with HTML in Canvas, which it says makes exports faster and higher fidelity, so compare a fresh export with an older one before reusing a preset.

Keep the publication state honest

Designing a website in Paper and publishing a functioning website are separate stages. The accepted design still needs implementation, hosting and verification at the destination. The exported code or local preview may be valuable progress, but it is not evidence that the public or private published URL serves the intended build. Inspect the delivered address and its important routes.

Paper’s email tutorial makes those stages visible. The agent created the template in Resend as a draft, warned that the logo still loaded from a Paper-hosted asset that should move to the sender’s own hosting before production, and noted that raw HTML is not editable in Resend’s visual editor until converted. A test send with sample variables came before publishing, and publishing a new version changes what is sent without code changes.

Give the deliverable an identifiable date or version so feedback refers to the right edition. Paper names each export after its frame and writes it to the Downloads folder, so rename and file it deliberately. Preserve the editable source alongside the finished output. A good publication should be useful now and straightforward to correct when content or product capabilities change.

In Paper

How it works in Paper

As of September 2026 the Export section at the bottom of the right panel exports a selection as PNG, JPG, AVIF, WebP or PDF at a chosen scale, one file per frame or one combined PDF, always into the Downloads folder. PDFs use the browser’s print engine, so text stays searchable. A copy icon in the same section puts a PNG, Tailwind or React CSS on the clipboard, and images and videos now render through HTML in Canvas.

Checked against the videos and documentation as of September 2026. Paper ships often; the release timeline in the reference shows what changed when.

Export one frame as a PDF

  1. Select the frame (the demo used a one-page resume, 612 × 792).
  2. Scroll to Export at the bottom of the right panel; if the section has no export row, click + to add one.
  3. Set the format dropdown to PDF. The scale field beside it read 1x.
  4. Optionally click the settings (sliders) icon: File suffix (empty, with the placeholder No suffix), Color space (sRGB), Quality (High, Medium or Low) and Image resampling (Detailed or Basic).
  5. Click Export ⇧⌘E. The PDF goes to Downloads, named after the frame.
⇧⌘E
Shown at 0:20

Export several frames, separate or combined

  1. Select all the frames (the demo: four 1920 × 1080 slides in one row).
  2. With PDF as the format, the Export section shows two buttons: Export 4 elements writes one PDF per frame; Export combined PDF writes one multi-page file.
  3. Click Export combined PDF. A toast reads Exported 1 file to Downloads; the file is Combined.pdf, 554 KB for the four slides.
  4. Pages follow the frames’ positions on the canvas, not the layer list: the title slide, last in the layers panel but first on the left, became page 1.
Shown at 1:08

Check the exported PDF

  1. Open the file in Preview and check the page count and order in the sidebar.
  2. Press ⌘F and search a word from the design; the demo’s search for quality found one match, on page 3, which shows the text is real text.
  3. Zoom on the smallest labels and on images, whose quality depends on the Image resampling setting.
  4. Optionally give the PDF to an AI assistant. Asked for a one-sentence summary, Claude correctly described single, separate and combined export and the adjustable settings.
⌘F
Shown at 1:22

Export an image at a chosen scale

  1. Select the frame or layer and go to Export in the right panel.
  2. Set the scale field (2x in the June 2026 changelog demo) and choose PNG, JPG, AVIF or WebP in the format dropdown.
  3. Click Export; each selected element becomes its own file in Downloads.
  4. Use + beside Export to add an export row and − to remove one.
Shown at 4:24

Copy to the clipboard instead of exporting a file

  1. Select the layer.
  2. Click the copy icon beside Export in the right panel, or right-click and open Copy as…
  3. Choose Copy as PNG (⇧⌘C) for an image, or Copy as Tailwind (⌥T) or Copy as React CSS (⌥R) for code.
  4. Paste it where it is needed: a message, a document or your code editor.
⇧⌘C⌥T⌥R
Shown at 3:53

Turn a frame into a sendable email template

  1. Finish the email frame in Paper and copy its link with Copy link (⌘L) at the top of the right panel.
  2. In an agent session that has Paper’s plugin and the email service’s plugin (Resend’s in the demo), ask it to make the frame a Resend template and paste the link.
  3. Approve the Paper tool calls; the agent first loads Paper’s instructions with get_guide, then the provider’s skill.
  4. The agent rebuilds the design as table-based email HTML, turns values that change per email into variables ({{{RESET_URL}}}, {{{RESEND_UNSUBSCRIBE_URL}}}), creates the template as a draft and returns a preview link.
  5. In Resend, convert the HTML to the visual editor if others will edit it, set the sender and subject, and send a test with Test variables as JSON, such as {"RESET_URL": "https://resend.com"}.
  6. Move images that still load from Paper to your own hosting, then publish; a template must be published before it can be sent.
Shown at 5:34

Limits and what is coming

  • Exports always go to the Downloads folder, named after the frame (Combined.pdf for a combined PDF); neither the app nor the MCP export tools choose a folder, as of September 2026.
  • SVG export works only for SVG layers, per Paper’s MCP export tool; frames export as PNG, JPG, AVIF, WebP or PDF.
  • Video export requires the Pro plan, per Paper’s pricing page in early October 2026.
  • Email clients need table-based HTML: the agent and the email service convert Paper’s HTML and CSS, and images may still load from Paper-hosted URLs that should move to your own hosting before production.

Build it in Paper

  1. Lay out the frames in reading order on the canvas, left to right, at page proportions (612 × 792 for a letter page, 1920 × 1080 for a slide), and name each frame the way its file should be named.
  2. Select them, scroll to Export at the bottom of the right panel and set the format to PDF; in the settings (sliders) icon choose Quality and Image resampling, plus an optional File suffix.
  3. Click Export combined PDF for one document, or Export N elements for one file per frame (Export ⇧⌘E for a single frame); the file lands in Downloads.
  4. Open the file: check page order, zoom on the smallest labels, search a distinctive word with ⌘F and test any links.
  5. For an email, give the frame’s Paper link (Copy link, ⌘L) to an agent with the email service’s tools, then preview, send a test with sample variables and publish only after it passes.

Check before you move on

  • Are the frames on the canvas in the order the pages should read?
  • Did you open the exported file and find a distinctive word with search?
  • Are the smallest labels readable at the size the reader will use?
  • Do the images and links in the delivered artifact load from where they will live, not from the Paper file?
  • Is the delivered version dated or versioned, with the editable source kept beside it?

Common mistakes

Ordering slides in the layers panel and expecting the combined PDF to follow it.

Arrange the frames on the canvas; combined PDFs follow canvas position (left to right in the demo; Paper’s MCP tool orders top to bottom, then left to right).

Exporting a wide screen frame as a document page.

Build a page-proportioned frame, such as 612 × 792 or 1920 × 1080, with type sized for reading, and export that instead.

Publishing an email whose images still load from Paper.

Ask the agent to list asset URLs, host the images yourself, and send a test with sample variables before publishing.

Looking for exports in the project folder.

Exports land in Downloads under the frame’s name; rename and move the file as part of the export step.

R1 · What shipped, month by month

60 releases from March to September 2026, and 37 features announced but not yet shipped.

March 6

  • Constraints panel — Layers outside Flex flow gained constraints that decide how they respond when their parent is resized.
  • Fit and Fill by double-click — Double-clicking a frame's edge or handle resizes it to fit its content, and ⌥ + double-click makes it fill its parent.
  • Backdrop filters — Layers can filter whatever sits behind them, as CSS backdrop-filter does.
  • OpenType features panel — Text gained a panel for turning on a font's OpenType features.
  • Lower memory use — The March release cut Paper's memory use.
  • Paper MCP server in Paper Desktop — Paper Desktop runs a local MCP server that coding agents connect to; the first setup tutorial linked Claude Code over HTTP and confirmed it with /mcp.

April 9

  • Paper Snapshot — A Chrome extension copies part or all of a live web page into Paper as editable HTML and CSS layers; the first tutorial followed on 2 May.
  • Teams with Editor and Admin roles — Teams can invite members as Editors or Admins, and people outside the team get view-only access.
  • New image and SVG models — GPT Image 2, Nano Banana 2 and Quiver Arrow 1.1 joined the generation models.
  • Shortcuts for generation and upload — ⇧⌘I opens image generation, ⇧⌘J SVG generation and ⇧⌘K uploads images from disk.
  • Agents can move layers — A new MCP tool lets agents reorder and reparent layers, alongside a refined system prompt for agents.
  • Text formatting shortcuts — Shortcuts step font size, weight, letter spacing and line height, and ⌘B and ⌘I toggle bold and italic.
  • Gem Smoke shader — A logo animation shader that reacts to the shape it is given joined the library.
  • Refreshed interface and H for panning — The interface was refreshed, and H selects the hand tool for panning the canvas.
  • Memory down 10 to 20 percent — A further release reduced memory use by 10 to 20 percent.

May 9

  • Copy and paste from Figma — Layers copied in Figma paste into Paper as editable layers with their SVGs and images; a beta tutorial followed on 3 June.
  • PDF export — Frames export as searchable PDFs, one per frame or combined into one file, saved to the Downloads folder.
  • Agents create and open files — New MCP tools let an agent create a Paper file, open existing files and change pages instead of working only in the open file.
  • Paste HTML as layers — HTML with inline styles pastes onto the canvas as editable layers.
  • Other styles panel — CSS that Paper renders but has no dedicated control for, often added by agents, appears in an Other styles panel.
  • Guests, follow mode and cursor chat — Files support view-only access and anonymous visitors, you can follow a collaborator's view, and / opens cursor chat.
  • Minimal interface — ⇧. collapses the panels into floating controls, leaving more of the canvas visible.
  • Full-page Snapshot — ⌘Return in the Snapshot extension captures an entire page, with a progress percentage.
  • Grok image model from xAI — Grok joined the image models; in the tutorial it returned a 4:3 image in about two seconds.

June 10

  • Negative gap — Flex gap accepts negative values, so children can overlap.
  • Higher-fidelity PDFs — PDF export began keeping shadows, gradients and blend modes.
  • Presence for teammates and agents — Files show who is present, including agents at work.
  • SVG editing and the pen tool — Paths inside SVGs can be edited node by node and the pen tool (P) draws new ones, released as a beta.
  • Top-layer hover selection — Hover now targets the top-level parent as in Figma; double-click or hold ⌘ to go deeper, or turn on Use deep selection.
  • Layer picker on ⌘ + right-click — Holding ⌘ and right-clicking lists every layer under the pointer, down to the smallest shape.
  • Folders and nested folders — The dashboard's Files view gained folders that nest to any depth, with Move to and rename.
  • Design tokens through the MCP — Agents create tokens from a codebase's CSS variables or from the canvas, with types modeled on Tailwind; at first the MCP was the only way to create them.
  • Copy tokens between files — Copy theme and Paste theme, in the menu under the Paper logo, move a file's tokens into another file.
  • Collapse all layers and resizable panels — Right-click in the layers list to collapse all layers, and drag to resize the left panel and the pages list.

July 1

  • Paper Shaders open source and free — Paper's shader library became open source and free to use in websites, apps, templates and plugins.

August 11

  • Tabs in the desktop app — Several files open as tabs, and + in the tab bar opens a new or existing file.
  • Agents across open files — Agents can work in any open file, including background tabs, so prompts should name the target file.
  • Tokens in the Theme tab — Tokens of every type can be created and edited in the left panel's Theme tab, and edits update every layer that uses them.
  • Favorite fonts — Starred fonts appear in a Favorites tab wherever you pick a font, including token editors.
  • Flex wrap — Children of a Flex frame can break onto new lines, chosen with Wrap in the Flex section's menu.
  • Repeatable duplicates — After an ⌥-drag duplicate with a rotation, ⌘D repeats both the offset and the rotation.
  • Dashboard multi-select and file duplication — ⌘-click selects several files and folders to move, archive or copy links, and files can be duplicated.
  • Free editors and viewer roles — Free plans allow unlimited editors, and viewer seats are free on every plan.
  • Comments — Press C to comment anywhere, then reply, react and resolve, with a panel that searches, sorts and filters threads in comment mode.
  • Comments as agent instructions — You can leave comments on a frame and ask an agent to implement them.
  • Lens Distortion shader — An image filter that bends geometry and splits color channels like a camera lens, usable on any layer including text.

September 14

  • WebMCP in the browser — Paper on the web added WebMCP support for agents that run in the browser.
  • CJK word-keeping — Text wrapping can keep Chinese, Japanese and Korean words intact.
  • Faster performance — Paper uses about half its previous memory, switches tabs faster and pans and zooms more smoothly on large files.
  • One-click agent setup — A Connect your agent button in the right panel sets up the Paper MCP for Cursor, Claude, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, VS Code, OpenCode, Codex, Codex CLI or Antigravity, with an Other agents option for the rest.
  • Image generation through the MCP — Agents can generate images on the canvas; asked for a variety pack, one produced four labeled images from OpenAI Image 2.5, Nano Banana 2, Flux 2 Pro and Recraft V4.1.
  • Opacity tokens — Opacity is a token type that pairs with a color token in a fill, for example the ink color at 60%.
  • Color tokens from a fill — The token icon beside a fill's color has a + that turns the raw value into a new color token; the build log says this works from any color field.
  • Token picker views — Color tokens in a fill's token menu can be shown as a list, a small grid or a large grid.
  • Dashboard search across folders — Dashboard search (⌘F) looks through every folder and opens results directly.
  • Personal drafts — The September dashboard shows a Drafts section and a Scratchpad file labeled as your permanent draft, after drafts were announced as next on 12 August; the video does not narrate it.
  • Reworked flex panel — Agent-built Flex layouts open in the panel, Space between sits beside the gap field, wrapped layouts get separate horizontal and vertical gaps, and grid elements support alignment and gap.
  • Copy as code from the Export section — A copy icon beside Export offers Copy as PNG (⇧⌘C), Copy as Tailwind (⌥T) and Copy as React CSS (⌥R), the options already in the right-click menu.
  • HTML in Canvas rendering — Images and videos are now powered by HTML in Canvas, which makes exports faster and higher fidelity.
  • Paper Texture shader rebuilt — The shader was rebuilt for rendering quality and speed, with more controls and new textures such as wrinkles, folds and crumples.

R4 · When something goes wrong

Symptoms, likely causes and the fix that works.

ProblemLikely causeFix
The agent says Paper is not connected, or Paper tools fail.Paper Desktop is not running, or no design file is open in it. The MCP server lives in the desktop app; a file open in a browser, or the desktop dashboard alone, does not count. With the Paper CLI setup the tools can stay listed while the app is closed, so a listed tool does not prove Paper is reachable.Open Paper Desktop on the target design file and try again. If the client still reports Paper as disconnected, restart the agent session.
Paper’s tools are missing right after setup, or the agent calls tools that do not exist.The server was added while the session was already running, so its tools were never loaded, or the session or its host app holds a stale tool list.Restart the agent session; in Claude Code, close and reopen it, then check /mcp or claude mcp list. If that is not enough, restart the host app, and if the agent still invents tools, restart everything. In Cursor, reload the window or toggle the server off and on in Cursor Settings › Tools & MCP.
Paper appears twice in a client’s MCP settings, or behaves differently from one session to the next.An older HTTP entry (http://127.0.0.1:29979/mcp, used in spring 2026 tutorials) and a newer Paper CLI entry are both configured.Keep one Paper entry per client. Follow the current setup in Paper’s docs or the Connect your agent dialog, and migrate the old entry instead of keeping both.
The agent edits the wrong file.Several files are open as tabs and the prompt named none, or it said “the active Paper file” and the tab in front changed before the agent started.Name the file or paste its link (Copy link, ⌘L) in the prompt. When you rely on the active file, stay on its tab until the agent’s dots appear there, and check the file name in the agent’s first reply.
The agent overwrites or ignores changes you made by hand.Agents do not track manual edits; they work from what they last read.Ask the agent to re-read the canvas, or the specific frame, before its next change.
A recolor misses icons or changes the wrong layers.Color searches can return false matches and miss vector details: in Paper’s tabs demo, a search for #000000 matched zero values, and SVG icon strokes did not show up in the agent’s color searches.Ask the agent to confirm each match by reading the subtree (get_jsx) or the computed styles, to check SVG strokes and fills explicitly, and to show a screenshot of the icons in the result.
Agent screenshots time out, or come back too small to judge.Screenshots are size-capped, and capturing a page with many boards, or one very large artboard, can be slow enough to time out (a viewer report answered by the Paper team).Name the frame or section to capture rather than the whole page. Ask for scale 2 only when small text must be readable, and ask for computed styles or JSX, not pixel reading, when you need exact sizes and colors.
Agent tool calls stop working after heavy use, or limits do not reset after upgrading.The Free plan allows 100 MCP tool calls per week (Pro: 1 million, per Paper’s pricing page in early October 2026), and an outdated desktop app can keep the old limit after an upgrade.Use Pro for sustained agent work. If limits do not reset after upgrading, update Paper Desktop (Check for Updates) and restart it.
The agent cannot reach Paper from WSL, or from behind a VPN or proxy.Without mirrored networking, WSL may not reach the desktop app running on Windows; a proxy or VPN can block Paper’s domains.In WSL, set networkingMode to mirrored. Behind a proxy or VPN, allowlist *.paper.design.
A Remote Control session stops responding while you are away from the computer.The computer went to sleep, or the session was not started from a Claude Code terminal session (a requirement as of July 2026).Start /remote-control (or /rc) in a terminal session, keep Paper Desktop open on the file, and in System Settings › Lock Screen set both display-off timers longer than you will be away (For 3 hours in Paper’s demo).
Content clips at the bottom of an agent-built artboard.The artboard has a fixed height that is too small for its content.Ask the agent to set the artboard height to fit-content with update_styles rather than guessing a taller fixed height, then take a new screenshot. By hand, double-click the frame’s bottom edge to fit its height to the content.
Text renders in the wrong font or weight.The family or weight is not installed on the computer and is not on Google Fonts, or the agent styled text without checking availability.Ask the agent to check families with get_font_family_info before styling (Paper’s server instructions require it once per session) and to prefer fonts already used in the file. Install missing fonts locally.
Local images are missing from a Snapshot capture of a site running on your machine.The development server blocks cross-origin requests from Paper; Vite 6 and later also block /@fs/ paths.Allow the origin https://app.paper.design in the dev server (Paper’s docs give settings for Astro, Django, Express, Fastify, Flask, Next.js, Nuxt, Rails, Vite, Remix, SvelteKit and webpack) and serve assets from public/.
You cannot find an exported file, or want an image without saving a file.Paper saves exports straight to the Downloads folder (documented for PDF in the May 2026 build log), and the MCP export tool has no destination option.Look in Downloads. To skip the file, use Copy as PNG (⇧⌘C) from the copy icon beside Export in the right panel, or from the right-click Copy as… menu.
A token changed in one file but not in another.Token sets copied between files are independent copies, not a linked library.Treat one file, or the codebase, as the source of truth and update the other files explicitly, by hand or by asking an agent to read the source and apply the changes.
A shader preset or code snippet no longer matches a tutorial.The shader packages are at version 0.0.x and can change between releases; Paper Texture’s parameters were reworked in 0.0.81 (September 2026).Pin the exact package version, check the effect’s current page on shaders.paper.design, and follow the Paper Texture migration guide when upgrading.

R5 · Briefs for your agent

Copy one into Claude Code, Cursor or any MCP client connected to Paper, then fill in the brackets.

Audit a frame before editing

Before any agent changes an existing frame, when you want a read-only diagnosis you can approve first.

Load the Paper guide if you have not this session. Work only in the Paper file "<file name or pasted link>", on the frame "<frame name>" (or my current selection). Do not change anything in this pass. First confirm which file, page and frame you are reading. Then read the frame with get_tree_summary, take one screenshot of that frame only, and read exact values with get_computed_styles and get_tokens. Report the fonts, sizes and weights in use; every color and whether it comes from a token; the spacing and alignment rules you can infer; layers with generic names; and any text that clips. Finish with the three problems that most hurt this screen's task, each with the change you propose and why. Wait for my approval before writing.
Explore N directions on separate artboards

When you want distinct alternatives to compare side by side without touching the original.

In the Paper file "<file>", explore <3> directions for the frame "<frame name>" and leave the original untouched. Before writing, list every action and content block on the original, then give each direction a short name, a one-line idea, its palette as hex values and its layout change, and wait for my go-ahead. Keep fixed in every direction: the logo, the navigation items, all listed actions, the real content and these fonts: <fonts>. Vary hierarchy and layout, not only color. Create one artboard per direction beside the original, at its size, named "<frame name> — 01 <direction>" and so on. Build breadth-first: the same section on every artboard before the next one. Screenshot each artboard and check it against the action list. If a tool call fails, tell me which artboard is incomplete. Call finish_working_on_nodes at the end.
Import code tokens into Paper

When the codebase already defines CSS variables and the Paper file should use the same values.

Create tokens in the open Paper file "<file>" from the CSS variables in this codebase, starting with <path, for example src/styles/>. Run get_tokens first and reuse any token that already exists; never duplicate one. Keep each variable's name where possible, keep aliases as var(--…) references to their base tokens, and create the tokens in batches with create_tokens: colors first, then typography, radius and spacing. If a value cannot be stored as written, such as light-dark() or calc(), do not guess: tell me which value you stored. End with a table of source file, variable, token, value and any conflict. Then build a "Style Guide" artboard that shows every token through var() so I can check the result on the canvas.
Implement an accepted frame in an existing codebase

When one frame is approved and should become production code that follows the repository's conventions.

Build the frame "<exact frame name>" from the open Paper file "<file>" into <path/to/file>. It is the accepted design; ignore every other variant. Read it with get_screenshot, get_jsx and get_computed_styles, and use get_fill_image for images: take sizes and colors from those values, never from the screenshot. Follow this repository's conventions. Reuse existing components such as <component> instead of creating new ones, use the existing tokens or theme, and keep <behavior, for example the sticky header> consistent with <where it already exists in the app>. Ask me before deciding any behavior the design does not show. When you are done, run the app, screenshot the page at <width>, compare it with the Paper frame, and list the remaining differences and every file you changed.
Align a comparison

When a table, plan comparison or set of metric rows looks tidy but values do not line up across rows.

In the Paper file "<file>", make the comparison in the frame "<frame name>" readable across rows. Read it first with get_tree_summary and one screenshot. Put every row on shared lanes: a label lane and one lane per compared value, each with a fixed width and flexShrink 0, so columns line up whatever the content. Left-align labels, right-align numbers, keep units attached to their values and use tabular figures if the font has them. Edit the existing nodes; do not regenerate the frame. Then stress-test a duplicate named "<frame name> — stress" with one very long label, one missing value shown explicitly rather than as zero, and one number with more digits than the rest. Screenshot after every three rows and at the end, and report any lane that still drifts.
Generate a token theme

When a file needs a token system built from an existing design before more screens are added.

In the Paper file "<file>", build a token theme from the frame "<reference frame>". Run get_tokens first and reuse anything that exists. Propose the set before creating it, in Tailwind v4 namespaces: --color-* (semantic roles such as background, surface, text, muted, border and accent before the raw palette), --font-*, --text-*, --leading-*, --tracking-* in em, --radius-*, --spacing-* and --breakpoint-*. Take every value from the reference with get_computed_styles; invent nothing. After I approve, create the tokens with create_tokens, aliasing with var(--…) where one token derives from another. Build a "Style Guide" artboard beside the reference that uses only var() references, then rebind the reference frame's colors and type to the tokens. Paper has no theme modes yet, so put any dark values in a separately named set and apply them to a duplicate of the frame.
Prepare an export

Before handing finished frames to someone outside Paper as PDF, PNG, SVG or video.

In the Paper file "<file>", prepare <frame names> for <destination, for example a client PDF>. Do not change the designs. Check each frame first for clipped text, missing images, images still generating (exports do not wait for them) and the smallest text size, and tell me what you find. For a multi-page PDF, list the frames in the order export_combined_pdf will use, which is canvas position from top to bottom, then left to right, and tell me if any frame needs moving. Then export with the default settings unless I give a format and scale, for example png at 2x. SVG export works only for SVG nodes. Report the file names and where they were saved. I will open the output to check page order, image quality and searchable text.
Review drift across parallel agents' artboards

After several agents have worked in parallel, before you choose, combine or port any of their frames.

Do not edit anything. In the Paper file "<file>", review the artboards <list them, or all artboards on page "<page>"> against the reference "<reference frame or style guide>" and these brand rules: fonts <fonts>, theme <light or dark>, colors only from the file's tokens. Use find_nodes and get_computed_styles to collect every font family, text size, color and radius in use. find_nodes can match substrings, so confirm each hit with get_computed_styles, and check SVG fills and strokes separately. Produce one table per artboard: property, expected value, value found, layers affected. Flag raw hex values that should be tokens, fonts that fell back to a default and any action present on the reference but missing here. Propose fixes grouped so that one agent can apply them, then wait for my approval.

R6 · Glossary

75 terms, each linked to the chapter that explains it.

Absolute position
A setting that takes a child out of its Flex frame's flow so it floats over the content and follows constraints. 04
Alias
A token whose value is another token, written var(--color-blue-500), so a semantic role follows its palette color. 05
Behavior state
An extra artboard that shows a non-default state, such as a scrolled header, so the implementer knows how the page should respond. 13
Brand drift
Output that departs from a brand's fonts, colors or theme, usually because the agent filled a gap in the brief with a default. 11
Breadcrumb
The folder path at the top of the dashboard (for example Files / Marketing / Social Media), used to move up a level or rename the current folder. 01
Breadth-first build
Building the same section on every variant before starting the next section, so all variants reach the same stage together. 11
Canonical frame
The single named frame that defines a pattern; specimens and variants are duplicated from it and judged against it. 12
Capture target
The element inside Snapshot’s blue box, which the ↑ and ↓ keys adjust before you capture. 08
Center
A constraint that keeps a layer's size and its centered position as the parent is resized. 04
Code component
A component defined in the codebase; an agent can rebuild it on Paper’s canvas as editable layers, but the copy is not linked to the code. 12
Combined PDF
One multi-page PDF built from several selected frames, one page per frame, ordered by position on the canvas. 14
Comment thread
A comment pinned to a layer, with its replies, reactions and an open or resolved status that people and agents can change. 10
Constraint
A rule that decides how a layer outside Flex flow keeps its position or size when its parent is resized. 04
Context image
An image selected while the Create image panel is open, which the next prompt edits instead of starting from scratch. 08
Contour
On logo animations, how far inside the shape pixels respond to its edge, from 0% (a plain mask) to 100% (edge-following bands throughout). 09
Copy as React CSS
Copies the selection as a React function whose elements carry inline style objects, headed by a comment with the layer’s Paper link and the date. 13
Deep selection
An optional hover mode, ticked in the file-name menu, in which the pointer targets the frame closest to the object under it. 01
Detach
Replacing a token on a property with its current literal value, which later token edits do not change. 05
Detached component
A Figma component or instance that arrives in Paper as plain layers, without its link to the main component. 08
Draft template
A Resend template that can be previewed and test-sent but must be published before it can be sent. 14
Encoding
The visual property that carries a value, such as position along a shared axis, length or color. 06
Fill
A size that takes the space the parent has left along that axis. 02
Fit
A size that follows the frame’s content, like CSS fit-content; the tutorial describes it as hugging the contents, and some tools call it Hug. 02
Fixed
A size you type or drag that does not respond to the content or to the parent. 02
Fixed, Fit and Fill
Paper's size modes: a set value, a size that hugs the contents, or a share of the parent's unused space. 03
Flex frame
A frame whose children are arranged by direction, gap, padding and alignment (CSS display: flex) instead of by coordinates. 02
Frame
Paper’s container layer, the equivalent of an HTML div; the layers inside it are its children. 01
Freeform frame
A frame without flex, whose children keep the positions you give them; the layers panel marks it with dashed corners. 01
Gap
The fixed space between neighboring children of a flex frame; with wrap on, the space between items and between lines is set separately. 02
get_computed_styles
The Paper MCP tool that returns the computed CSS of layers, the source of exact values for code. 13
get_jsx
The Paper MCP tool that returns a layer subtree as JSX, styled with Tailwind classes by default or with inline styles. 13
Harness
The agent application a model runs in, such as Claude Code, Cursor or GitHub Copilot, which you choose when connecting Paper. 10
HTML in Canvas
The rendering method Paper adopted in September 2026 for images and videos, which it says makes exports faster and higher fidelity. 14
Image filter
A shader that transforms an input image, which can be any layer captured with the eyedropper, including text or another shader. 09
Image resampling
The PDF setting that processes images as Detailed (finer detail; Lanczos, per the MCP tool) or Basic (smaller files; Hamming). 14
Inline style
CSS written in an element’s style attribute, the only styling Paper’s HTML paste reads. 08
Lane
A position that the same kind of content occupies in every row, such as a label lane or a value lane of one fixed width. 03
Left + Right
A horizontal constraint that keeps fixed distances to both side edges, so the layer's width changes with its parent. 04
Logo animation
A shader (Heatmap, Liquid Metal or Gem Smoke) whose animated pattern is shaped by the edges of a supplied logo or built-in shape. 09
Magic Swatches
The freeform frame that Extract colors creates from an image, holding 100 × 60 rectangles named by their hex values. 01
MCP
Model Context Protocol: the interface through which an agent reads and writes the open Paper file with tools such as get_jsx and write_html. 13
MCP server
A connector that lets an agent read or write another system, such as Notion or a Paper file. 06
Mirrored handles
A node’s two curve handles moving symmetrically; hold ⌥ to move one alone and ⌘ to mirror them again. 07
Opacity token
A percentage token, added in September 2026, that can be paired with a color token in a fill’s percentage field. 05
Paper CLI
A command-line program, run with the argument mcp, that relays a client’s stdio connection to Paper Desktop; Paper’s docs name it as the current way to connect most clients. 10
Paper Snapshot
Paper’s Chrome extension that captures a page region or a whole page and pastes it into Paper as editable HTML/CSS layers. 08
Path
One editable vector shape inside an SVG, with its own nodes, fill and stroke. 07
Preset
A named set of parameter values, such as Warp’s Cauldron Pot, that replaces all current values when clicked. 09
Reference mark
A target, baseline or threshold drawn so that it cannot be mistaken for a measured value. 06
Remote Control
A Claude Code feature, started with /remote-control or /rc, that lets the Claude mobile app continue a session running on your computer. 10
Searchable PDF
A PDF whose text is stored as text rather than pixels, so people and tools can search, select and read it. 14
Shader
A small GPU program that computes the color of every pixel; in Paper it is a layer whose look comes from a preset, parameters and colors, rendered live with WebGL2. 09
Shared scale
One mapping from value to length that every comparable mark uses, so equal lengths always mean equal values. 06
Sibling
A layer that shares its parent with another layer; siblings move with the parent and follow its layout rules. 01
Silhouette
An asset’s overall outline, which must stay recognizable at its smallest display size. 07
Slot
In component systems, a named region that accepts different content in each use; Paper’s roadmap listed components with slots as coming soon in September 2026. 12
Space between
An alignment that pushes the first and last children to the ends and spreads the rest evenly (CSS justify-content: space-between). 02
Specimen
A copy of the canonical frame filled with a demanding case, such as long text, missing data or a selected state, to test the pattern’s limits. 12
Speed
A shader’s animation rate, shown in percent in Paper and as a multiplier in code; 0 stops the animation loop and leaves a still frame. 09
Steer
Sending a message into an agent's current run so it changes course immediately, as opposed to queuing it until the run ends. 11
Stretch
A constraint that scales a layer's size and its distances to the edges in proportion, shown as a percentage width. 04
Stroke position
Whether a path’s stroke paints above its fill, centered on the edge, or below it, so that it reads as an outside outline. 07
SVG container
The outer SVG layer in Paper, which behaves like a frame, holds Path layers and clips them at its edges. 07
Tabular numerals
Digits that all share one width, so numbers with the same count of digits line up in a column. 03
Template variable
A placeholder such as {{{RESET_URL}}} that the email service fills with a real value when it sends. 14
Theme
Paper’s name for a file’s set of tokens, as in the Copy theme and Paste theme commands. 05
Token
A named value stored in a Paper file as a CSS custom property, such as --color-accent, that layers reference with var(). 05
Translation layer
A conversion step between a design format and code; Paper has none because its canvas is HTML and CSS. 13
Variable font
A font with continuous axes such as weight and optical size, so any value in its range can be set. 05
Variant
A duplicate that changes one rule of the pattern, named after that change and kept beside the original for comparison. 12
Variety pack
Create image’s default option, which sends one prompt to four models and returns four images. 08
Vector editing mode
The state, entered by double-clicking a selected path, in which its nodes and curve handles can be moved. 07
Working indicator
The animated dots Paper shows on a tab and above an artboard while an agent is working there. 10
Workspace (Conductor)
An isolated copy of the repository on its own branch, so agents in different workspaces cannot overwrite each other's code. 11
Wrap
A Flex setting that lets children break onto new lines instead of shrinking or overflowing, like CSS flex-wrap. 04

Further reading

Seven authors to read next.

Seven books offer seven ways to question a design: its rules, alignment, encoding, evidence, color, reading rhythm and purpose. Their ideas are summarized here in our own words; read the books for the real thing.

One composition, three lessons

Share an edge.

A common edge turns separate pieces into one composition. Change the rule and watch the relationships move.

Karl Gerstner

Designing Programmes · 1964

Swiss graphic designer and artist who developed systematic approaches to typography, identity and composition.

Describing the problem precisely is already part of solving it.

A reusable design starts with a precise problem: which content varies, which relationships stay fixed, and how the reader will use them. Treat a layout as a programme of explicit choices (where the label, value, unit and comparison go) before you make the second card. Variation then becomes a controlled response to content rather than improvisation.

Try it in Paper

Make one comparison row with a label lane and two equal value lanes. Duplicate it into compact and spacious versions, changing only padding and gap. Add a long label to both and keep the rules that survive.

Related: chapter 12, Reuse

Josef Müller-Brockmann

Grid Systems in Graphic Design · 1981

Swiss graphic designer whose teaching and books made the grid a practical method for organizing visual communication.

Choosing a grid is choosing to systematize, and so to clarify.

A grid's value is the reading path it creates. A common left edge makes labels easy to scan; a common right edge makes quantities easy to compare. A row should take its positions from the shared structure, not from the length of its current label, and an orderly screen still needs exceptions when the content or task changes.

Try it in Paper

Rebuild three rows as a vertical Flex stack with identical label, bar and value widths. Change 56.2K to 156.2K and lengthen one label, then check whether the invisible structure still holds.

Related: chapter 03, Alignment

Jacques Bertin

Semiology of Graphics · 1967

French cartographer and theorist who studied how graphic variables carry different kinds of information.

Every component of data is qualitative, ordered or quantitative, and each kind needs different visual variables.

A name identifies a category, a rank gives an order, a share gives an amount. A visual treatment should preserve the relationship it claims to show: equal identity treatment for names can sit beside bars whose lengths encode different shares, but a change of shade alone cannot communicate an exact ratio.

Try it in Paper

Take three options A, B and C at 42%, 35% and 23%. Give them equal labelled marks for identity, then add horizontal bars on one scale for quantity, sorted by share. Say what each visual variable now means.

Related: chapter 06, Information

Edward R. Tufte

The Visual Display of Quantitative Information · 1983

Statistician and author whose books examine how graphics support reasoning about evidence.

Above everything else, a display should show the data.

A display earns its space by helping someone judge evidence. Removing a heavy border may help; removing the unit or an uncertainty note harms the same task. Motion should explain a change or preserve continuity, not compete with the reading.

Try it in Paper

Duplicate a comparison card. In the copy, remove the shadow, the enclosure and redundant labels, but keep the unit, the baseline and the comparison. Compare both at phone width and restore any cue whose removal made the meaning harder to recover.

Related: chapter 06, Information

Josef Albers

Interaction of Color · 1963

Artist and teacher whose color exercises grew out of direct observation at Black Mountain College and Yale.

Color is relative: the same color reads differently with every change of surrounding.

A grey token has no fixed visual strength. The same mark looks lighter, darker or more prominent depending on its surface, which matters in a monochrome interface: a selected state must stay clear on the page ground and on a white panel. This is perception, not a contrast check; text still needs a measured contrast ratio.

Try it in Paper

Place two identical #888888 squares, one on #EEEEEE and one on #535353. Keep size and fill identical and compare them. Then judge a selected row in its real context before you change its token.

Related: chapter 05, Tokens and type

Robert Bringhurst

The Elements of Typographic Style · 1992

Poet, translator and typographer whose work connects the craft of language with the form of the page.

Rhythm, proportion, structure and the choice of type have to be judged together.

A pleasant typeface cannot rescue an exhausting line length, and a bigger heading cannot repair a confused section structure. Adjust the measure and the line spacing before you add another container or label.

Try it in Paper

Set the same 120-word passage in two frames at the same size, one narrow and one wide, and adjust the line spacing in each. Read both aloud, keep the one where the next line is easiest to find, and check it again at phone width.

Related: chapter 05, Tokens and type

Stephen Few

Show Me the Numbers · 2012

Author and educator focused on the practical design of tables, graphs and analytical displays.

Different quantitative relationships call for different kinds of graphs.

The same values answer several questions. Someone looking up an exact quantity needs a different emphasis from someone looking for the biggest gap against a target. Name the decision first, then choose the arrangement that reveals it, with targets and actuals on one scale.

Try it in Paper

Show stock as an aligned row: 64 on hand, 24 incoming, target 100. Duplicate it as a bar ending at 88 with a target marker at 100. Compare which view supports exact lookup and which makes the 12-unit gap visible.

On the Snapshot capture, Harcourt prompts Claude Code in the Claude desktop app's Code tab (Sonnet 4.6, Auto accept edits) to add a third column using copy parked in a side frame. Earliest agent video (Paper Alpha). Stephen adds the Notion MCP to Claude Code next to the Paper MCP, checks both with /mcp (Notion: connected, authenticated, https://mcp.notion.com/mcp, 12 tools; actions View tools, Re-authenticate, Clear authentication, Reconnect, Disable), and asks Claude to design a Notion 'Core Values' page in Paper. The agent runs notion-search and Paper get_basic_info in parallel, notion-fetch, get_font_family_info for four families, writes a brief, creates an artboard and builds it with semantically named sections (Header, Core Values Section, Tactics Section, Reading Section, Footer). Works with any MCP source, web search, and data viz.

Written down in09 · Shaders

How this guide was made

All 52 entries on youtube.com/@paperdesign were downloaded with their captions. 51 have spoken captions; one Short is music only and was read from its frames. Every video was analysed from its transcript and from frames sampled every few seconds, and the procedures, control names and shortcuts in this guide were checked against those frames.

Paper's own documentation (agent setup, Snapshot, pasting from Figma and HTML, tokens, vector editing, the shader library and the public roadmap) supplied current facts. The principle chapters, studies and plates began as an illustrated book designed in Paper; this edition makes them general and adds the Paper detail.

Everything is dated September 2026. Paper changes quickly, so treat statuses and limits as a snapshot and check the build log for anything newer.

Learn Paper with me. An illustrated guide to Paper, September 2026 edition. Written by Enzo Simier with AI assistance, from Paper's public videos and documentation. Not affiliated with Paper. Paper Shaders © Paper, Apache License 2.0.
